Topic: Comparing health indicators with appropriate denominators
Prompt: A mortality comparison reports a standardized mortality ratio of 1.0. What does this say about observed and expected deaths?
Reason: The expectation already reflects the reference stratum-specific rates applied to the study population.
Source: Penn State STAT 507 · https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat507/Lesson03 · disease occurrence and standardization

Topic: Comparing health indicators with appropriate denominators
Prompt: Which three dimensions need defining before comparing an apparent disease cluster with an expected count?
Answer: Who is included, the geographic area and the time interval.
Reason: These define the population, place and period of comparison. A striking count without them is difficult to interpret.
Source: CDC, Updated Guidelines for Evaluating Public Health Surveillance Systems · https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/248461 · purpose, completeness and timeliness of reporting

Topic: Comparing health indicators with appropriate denominators
Prompt: A community alert lists dates of possible exposure but gives no action for people who meet the criteria. What essential part of the message is missing?
Answer: An explicit recommended action and where to obtain help.
Reason: Communicate what is known, identify who is affected and explain the next step.
Source: CDC, Updated Guidelines for Evaluating Public Health Surveillance Systems · https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/248461 · purpose, completeness and timeliness of reporting

Topic: Comparing health indicators with appropriate denominators
Prompt: Comparable groups show a risk ratio of 0.30 for vaccinated versus unvaccinated people over a season. How is relative vaccine effectiveness calculated?
Reason: State the outcome, population and period. The absolute benefit depends on baseline risk.
Source: CDC, Principles of Epidemiology · https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/csels/dsepd/ss1978/lesson3/ · measures of frequency, association and public health impact

Topic: Comparing health indicators with appropriate denominators
Prompt: A healthy-food program measures only nutrition knowledge even though residents describe the nearest affordable grocer as unreachable without a car. Which relevant determinant is unmeasured?
Answer: Physical access to affordable food, including transportation.
Reason: Knowledge alone cannot measure whether residents can obtain the food.
Source: CDC · https://www.cdc.gov/transportation/php/about/index.html · transportation policy and health access

Topic: Comparing health indicators with appropriate denominators
Prompt: A risk model uses prior hospitalization to predict readmission. Does predictive value by itself establish that the predictor causes the event?
Answer: No. Prediction alone does not establish causation.
Reason: It may mark underlying illness severity. A causal claim needs additional evidence.
Source: CDC, Principles of Epidemiology · https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/csels/dsepd/ss1978/lesson3/ · measures of frequency, association and public health impact

Topic: Comparing health indicators with appropriate denominators
Prompt: In a county, 900 younger residents have 9 events and 100 older residents have 10. What is the crude risk for the combined county?
Reason: 19/1,000 = 1.9%. An unweighted mean of age-specific risks ignores the different group sizes.
Source: Penn State STAT 507 · https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat507/Lesson03 · disease occurrence and standardization

Prompt: With reference age 75 and no discounting, two deaths occur at 25 and 70. How many years of potential life lost are counted?
Source: CDC, Principles of Epidemiology · https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/csels/dsepd/ss1978/lesson3/ · measures of frequency, association and public health impact

Topic: Comparing health indicators with appropriate denominators
Prompt: A town's age pyramid has a broad base and very narrow oldest bands. Which feature of the data supports prioritizing pediatric service capacity?
Answer: A large number or share in the youngest age groups.
Reason: Use absolute counts and local needs to size services. Shape alone does not determine all priorities.

Topic: Comparing health indicators with appropriate denominators
Prompt: A program sees fewer infections among unvaccinated infants after eligible older children are vaccinated. Which population effect could contribute?
Reason: A before-after pattern alone does not prove this explanation. Other time trends require evaluation.
Source: CDC, Principles of Epidemiology · https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/csels/dsepd/ss1978/lesson1/section10.html · chain of infection and herd immunity

Topic: Comparing health indicators with appropriate denominators
Prompt: A screening pilot recruits only people who can drive to a distant center during working hours. Which access barrier could bias the enrolled sample?
Answer: Transport and work-schedule requirements can exclude otherwise eligible people.
Reason: Compare participants with the source population and offer accessible recruitment options.
Source: CDC · https://www.cdc.gov/transportation/php/about/index.html · transportation policy and health access

Topic: Comparing health indicators with appropriate denominators
Prompt: Two hospitals each report one maternal death this year, but one has ten times as many live births. Why are raw counts inadequate for comparing maternal mortality?
Answer: Different birth denominators imply different maternal mortality ratios.
Reason: Small counts also produce imprecise estimates. Case mix and referral patterns matter.
Source: WHO · https://www.who.int/data/gho/indicator-metadata-registry/imr-details/26 · maternal mortality ratio

Topic: Comparing health indicators with appropriate denominators
Prompt: A report calls all deaths before the first birthday neonatal deaths. Which age group must be removed for a neonatal mortality indicator?

Topic: Comparing health indicators with appropriate denominators
Prompt: A stroke program reduces long-term disability without changing survival. Which population summary can register that benefit even if life expectancy stays fixed?
Answer: Healthy life expectancy or another disability-sensitive measure.
Reason: Survival alone misses years lived with impairment. A reduction in disability can also reduce DALYs lost.
Source: WHO Global Health Observatory · https://www.who.int/data/gho/data/indicators/indicator-details/GHO/gho-ghe-hale-healthy-life-expectancy · healthy life expectancy

Topic: Comparing health indicators with appropriate denominators
Prompt: A dashboard using a fixed age-75 cutoff assigns zero years of potential life lost to a death at 79. Does that imply the death caused no loss of health or well-being?
Answer: No. It reflects the selected cutoff in this metric.
Reason: Use complementary mortality, disability and quality-of-life measures when making policy decisions.

Topic: Comparing health indicators with appropriate denominators
Prompt: Reports of a rare diagnosis triple after the local laboratory changes its test and reporting policy. What should be verified before declaring a new disease cluster?
Answer: Whether the diagnosis and ascertainment are comparable before and after the change.
Reason: Use consistent case definitions, geography, time and population denominators.
Source: CDC, Updated Guidelines for Evaluating Public Health Surveillance Systems · https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/248461 · purpose, completeness and timeliness of reporting

Topic: Comparing health indicators with appropriate denominators
Prompt: Two clinics estimate the same vaccine effectiveness of 50%. Unvaccinated one-season risks are 10% and 2%. In which clinic is more absolute risk prevented per vaccinated person?
Reason: Assuming the relative effect transports, absolute reductions are 5 versus 1 percentage point. Indirect community effects are a separate question.
Source: CDC, Principles of Epidemiology · https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/csels/dsepd/ss1978/lesson3/ · measures of frequency, association and public health impact

Topic: Comparing health indicators with appropriate denominators
Prompt: A cafeteria report divides ill salad eaters by everyone in the building, including non-diners. Which denominator should estimate the salad-specific attack proportion?
Answer: All at-risk people who actually ate the salad during the relevant meal.
Reason: Use the corresponding exposed and unexposed denominators for the comparison.

Topic: Comparing health indicators with appropriate denominators
Prompt: A county has high average vaccine coverage but one neighborhood has low coverage. Why can the county average overstate protection for susceptible residents there?

Prompt: Two tests both measure the same biological marker. Can their false-positive probabilities automatically be multiplied to calculate the chance that both are positive in someone without disease?

Topic: Reading statistical error regions from a sampling model
Prompt: In a one-sided test rejecting for large estimates, which distribution supplies the upper-tail area called alpha?
Answer: The sampling distribution under the null hypothesis.

Topic: Reading statistical error regions from a sampling model
Prompt: The critical value is the vertical line. The shaded region is under the null curve, on the rejection side. Which error probability does it represent?
Answer: Alpha, the probability of a false positive under the null.
Reason: Repeated samples under the null fall to the right with probability alpha.
Source: ICH E9 · https://database.ich.org/sites/default/files/E9_Guideline.pdf · sections 3 and 5, trial size, estimation, multiplicity and subgroups

Topic: Reading statistical error regions from a sampling model
Prompt: Here the shaded region lies under the specified alternative curve on the nonrejection side. Which error probability is shown?
Answer: Beta, the probability of missing this true effect.

Topic: Reading statistical error regions from a sampling model
Prompt: For a fixed rejection threshold, shifting the alternative sampling distribution farther into the rejection region changes power in which direction?

Topic: Checking that the sampling frame matches the question

Topic: Interpreting sparse events and absolute benefit

Topic: Interpreting sparse events and absolute benefit

Topic: Weighting independent estimates in a synthesis

Topic: Weighting independent estimates in a synthesis
Prompt: Two comparable trials estimate a mean benefit of 2 and 6 points on the same scale. In a fixed-effect synthesis their normalized inverse-variance weights are 0.75 and 0.25. What is the pooled mean benefit?

Topic: Weighting independent estimates in a synthesis
Prompt: Two trials measure pain on different numeric scales that assess the same construct. What kind of continuous effect measure can put them on a common scale for synthesis?
Reason: Check direction and comparability of constructs and SDs. The standardization denominator is a within-study measure of spread.

Topic: Weighting independent estimates in a synthesis
Prompt: A reviewer assesses allocation, missing outcomes, measurement and selective reporting separately for one trial result. What systematic-review task is this?
Reason: Assess the risk that the particular result is distorted and explain the judgment within each domain.

Topic: Weighting independent estimates in a synthesis

Answer: To define which participants are eligible for enrollment.

Topic: Testing practical applicability of research evidence

Answer: How well it improves outcomes when delivered in usual practice.

Topic: Testing practical applicability of research evidence

Topic: Testing practical applicability of research evidence
Prompt: A study reports equal average symptom relief with a daily pill or weekly injection. What patient-specific information is needed before choosing between them?
Answer: The patient's preferences and practical constraints for each regimen, alongside harms and other outcome differences.
Reason: When average benefits are similar, treatment burden and route may matter substantially to the patient.
Source: Cochrane Handbook chapter 15 · https://www.cochrane.org/authors/handbooks-and-manuals/handbook/current/chapter-15 · absolute effects, applicability and implications for practice

Topic: Selecting a diagnostic strategy from patient-level evidence
Prompt: In a validation cohort 25 reference-positive patients test negative and 75 reference-positive patients test positive. What fraction of disease cases does the assay detect?

Topic: Selecting a diagnostic strategy from patient-level evidence
Prompt: A new population screen detects additional early cases but there is no accessible confirmatory pathway. What requirement for a useful screening program remains unmet?

Topic: Selecting a diagnostic strategy from patient-level evidence

Topic: Selecting a diagnostic strategy from patient-level evidence
Prompt: Replicate test readings agree, but comparison with the reference repeatedly misclassifies disease. Which property of the test remains poor?
Answer: Validity against the disease reference despite good repeatability.

Topic: Distinguishing risk prediction and population health loss
Prompt: A strong risk model includes a fixed patient characteristic. A colleague interprets its large coefficient as the expected benefit of changing that characteristic. What inference is unsupported?
Answer: A predictive association alone cannot identify the effect of an intervention.

Topic: Distinguishing risk prediction and population health loss
Prompt: A program reduces disability-weighted years by 80 with no change in years of life lost. What happens to DALYs lost, all else equal?

Topic: CARS · Humanities · Keeping a promptbook
Prompt:
At the first reading of a comedy, the director found a pause marked in the promptbook after a character announced that the house had been sold. A penciled note in the margin said “six seconds.” The production that supplied this book had been admired for the peculiar chill that passed through the room at precisely this moment. Our director set a watch on the rehearsal table. The actors waited six seconds. Nothing in particular happened.

The note had been written by a stage manager, who occupied a seat from which the room could be heard unusually well. She kept a record because the actor who spoke next had a habit of swallowing the first word of his line. At one performance the audience laughed at the announcement. The laugh grew, faltered as people understood who would lose their home, and went out in scattered coughs. Six seconds passed before the room was quiet enough for a softly spoken reply. The record was an accurate measurement of that evening. The difficulty arose when an accurate measurement was promoted to an instruction.

A sympathetic reader might replace “six seconds” with “wait for quiet.” That would work on an evening when the audience laughed. Yet on another evening silence fell at once. An actor who answered immediately made the reply sound like a practical objection to the sale. An actor who allowed the silence to sit for a moment made the same words sound like an acknowledgment of grief. Quiet supplied an opportunity to speak, but it did not choose between those meanings.

It is tempting to conclude that nothing worth preserving can be written down. The company's understudy offers a reason for resisting that conclusion. She had never seen the celebrated performance. The stage manager's note made her ask why anyone would count the interval at all. In answering, her colleagues recalled that the announcement had once been played as a joke and the reply had interrupted the laughter. That earlier failure was useful to her. Having heard what the actors had once overlooked, she could listen for it herself. A record may do its best work by provoking a question that its maker had no occasion to put on paper.

I would keep the number in a new promptbook, accompanied by the reason it had been measured. I would also keep the director's unsuccessful rehearsal with the watch. It shows a future company how easily a description can acquire authority when it sits beside an actor's line. Such a book will sometimes disappoint a reader looking for a way to recover the experience of one remarkable night. But a company does not need to reproduce the six seconds in order to inherit something from that night. It can inherit the responsibility for deciding what the coming reply will sound like to the people actually in the room.

What was the stage manager originally using the six-second interval to document?
Choices:
How long it took for the audience to understand the sale
When the next line could be heard clearly at one performance
The duration the director thought necessary to suggest grief
The interval the actor normally preferred between lines
Answer: When the next line could be heard clearly at one performance
Reason: She was concerned that the first word was getting lost. The recorded interval ended when that evening’s audience was quiet enough to hear it.
Source: Original passage and item · AAMC CARS framework · https://students-residents.aamc.org/whats-mcat-exam/critical-analysis-and-reasoning-skills-section-overview

Topic: CARS · Humanities · Keeping a promptbook
Prompt:
At the first reading of a comedy, the director found a pause marked in the promptbook after a character announced that the house had been sold. A penciled note in the margin said “six seconds.” The production that supplied this book had been admired for the peculiar chill that passed through the room at precisely this moment. Our director set a watch on the rehearsal table. The actors waited six seconds. Nothing in particular happened.

The note had been written by a stage manager, who occupied a seat from which the room could be heard unusually well. She kept a record because the actor who spoke next had a habit of swallowing the first word of his line. At one performance the audience laughed at the announcement. The laugh grew, faltered as people understood who would lose their home, and went out in scattered coughs. Six seconds passed before the room was quiet enough for a softly spoken reply. The record was an accurate measurement of that evening. The difficulty arose when an accurate measurement was promoted to an instruction.

A sympathetic reader might replace “six seconds” with “wait for quiet.” That would work on an evening when the audience laughed. Yet on another evening silence fell at once. An actor who answered immediately made the reply sound like a practical objection to the sale. An actor who allowed the silence to sit for a moment made the same words sound like an acknowledgment of grief. Quiet supplied an opportunity to speak, but it did not choose between those meanings.

It is tempting to conclude that nothing worth preserving can be written down. The company's understudy offers a reason for resisting that conclusion. She had never seen the celebrated performance. The stage manager's note made her ask why anyone would count the interval at all. In answering, her colleagues recalled that the announcement had once been played as a joke and the reply had interrupted the laughter. That earlier failure was useful to her. Having heard what the actors had once overlooked, she could listen for it herself. A record may do its best work by provoking a question that its maker had no occasion to put on paper.

I would keep the number in a new promptbook, accompanied by the reason it had been measured. I would also keep the director's unsuccessful rehearsal with the watch. It shows a future company how easily a description can acquire authority when it sits beside an actor's line. Such a book will sometimes disappoint a reader looking for a way to recover the experience of one remarkable night. But a company does not need to reproduce the six seconds in order to inherit something from that night. It can inherit the responsibility for deciding what the coming reply will sound like to the people actually in the room.

Print the original tempo with a note that it allowed an echo to decay before the next entry.

Replace the original tempo with the mean tempo from several respected recordings.
Answer: Print the original tempo with a note that it allowed an echo to decay before the next entry.
Reason: The tempo and its purpose are both preserved, allowing performers to decide how to achieve audibility in another room.

Topic: CARS · Humanities · Rereading a clue
Prompt:
Halfway through a short detective story, a landlady tells her visitor that the tenant upstairs has finally gone home. The sentence costs a translator an afternoon. In the language of the story the landlady uses a form of address that suggests a previous acquaintance with her visitor. It would be an odd form to use with a stranger, although a woman of her age might use it with someone considerably younger. The visitor's age has yet to be mentioned. Two pages later, when we learn that the visitor is her son, the landlady's speech sounds quite ordinary. A reader who happened to notice it on the first encounter may enjoy having noticed it. A reader who passed it by can later find it waiting on the page.

The translator's language supplies no corresponding distinction in its pronouns. One solution is to let the landlady call her visitor “dear.” But imagine the visitor addressed that way in a story full of brisk professional exchanges. What had been an unobtrusive irregularity might become the only conspicuously intimate word on the page. Another solution is to omit the distinction. The disclosure of the visitor's identity would still surprise, yet on returning to the scene a reader would find nothing there to reconsider. Both solutions preserve what the landlady tells the visitor about the tenant. They offer rather different terms on which a reader may come to know the landlady.

A third translator lets the landlady interrupt the visitor before he has quite finished explaining why he came. Several other conversations in the story have made a point of observing formal courtesies. Breaking that rhythm here gives a reader a small reason to suspect familiarity. An impatient landlady has ample reason to interrupt a stranger, too. The device borrows no particular word from the original. Its defense is that it permits two readings before the disclosure and makes one of them especially satisfying afterward.

It would be a mistake to turn this defense into a general license to put interruptions wherever a translator has lost a nuance. Suppose the landlady's unfailing courtesy, even under provocation, is what later persuades a witness to trust her. An interruption could then repair a local difficulty at the expense of a more distant part of the story. Before deciding how much ingenuity a sentence will bear, one has to ask what else the proposed solution obliges the book to say.

Nor would a survey showing equal numbers of surprised readers settle the matter. Two readers can be equally astonished by a revelation, yet only one may feel invited to turn back a page. If I could ask those readers a second question, I would ask what they hoped to find when they turned back. A translation owes something to that return journey. A clue that everyone sees at once, and a clue that nobody could possibly have seen, each affords the reader rather little occasion to make it.

What feature of the landlady’s original form of address matters most to the author?
Choices:
It creates a clue whose importance can change on rereading.
It tells the visitor more about the missing tenant than the narrator knows.
It identifies the visitor’s age more reliably than his relationship.
It marks a level of intimacy that a first-time reader must recognize.
Answer: It creates a clue whose importance can change on rereading.
Reason: The address initially admits more than one explanation. After the family relationship is disclosed, a reader can recover the clue.

Topic: CARS · Social science · The night watch
Prompt:
The cooperative that shared a kiln among the potters of a coastal town had no official night watch. Somebody nevertheless had to stay with a firing until the kiln could safely be left. A potter might volunteer because a neighbor had covered for her last winter, because his own pots occupied most of the shelves, or because the other potters had small children. Asked who owed whom a night, members would usually name several considerations and then admit that the considerations did not point in quite the same direction. An economist visiting the workshop described the result as a system of exchange without accounts. That was close enough to win nods from the members and imprecise enough to conceal their most interesting disagreement.

When the cooperative doubled in size, a treasurer proposed that one night on watch earn one credit. Anyone who had used up her credits would take the next available shift. The proposal appealed especially to newcomers. An established potter could decline a night with a two-word reference to a sick aunt. A newcomer with an equally sick relative might have to tell a long and embarrassing story before the request seemed reasonable. A credit in the book would entitle either to say no without giving an account of her household. It would be easy to mistake the old members' discretion for a courtesy that the new members enjoyed equally.

After a season of bookkeeping, however, two experienced members objected that the accounts omitted the work of instructing novices. Teaching someone to load the kiln might save the cooperative many spoiled firings, yet no credit was issued for it. The treasurer offered to add a column for instruction. This reply pleased the member who did most of the teaching. It failed to satisfy the other, who had never taught a novice. Her complaint was that the new arrangement settled in advance which acts the members could invoke when deciding a shift. Before the ledger, she said, a contribution that nobody had thought important on Monday could be recognized as decisive on Friday. With another column there would merely be two things the cooperative had already thought of on Monday.

The distinction is easy to miss if we ask members only whether they consider the distribution of nights fair. Both critics might give the same low rating, and the newcomer, glad of her credit, a high one. If the credit for teaching were introduced, a rise in the average rating could be perfectly genuine without answering the second critic. Her concern would be better tested by watching what happens the first time a member offers a reason for changing shifts that the ledger has no place to record.

Nothing in this account requires the cooperative to abandon credits. A member who can politely decline without describing an ill relative has gained something that a richer communal discussion would not supply. The choice worth investigating is whether a posted balance must settle every case, or whether a member may occasionally reopen a case without being forced to reopen the door to her private life.

What feature of the ledger concerns the critic who has never taught a novice?
Choices:
It places too little monetary value on the skilled work of teaching.
It makes the grounds for changing shifts depend on categories chosen in advance.
It gives newcomers more opportunities to decline a shift than established members.
It leaves the cooperative unable to determine how many shifts a member has worked.
Answer: It makes the grounds for changing shifts depend on categories chosen in advance.
Reason: Her objection concerns which reasons can be considered, including contributions that acquire significance only later.

A potter might volunteer because a neighbor had covered for her last winter, because his own pots occupied most of the shelves, or because the other potters had small children. Asked who owed whom a night, members would usually name several considerations and then admit that the considerations did not point in quite the same direction. An economist visiting the workshop described the result as a system of exchange without accounts. That was close enough to win nods from the members and imprecise enough to conceal their most interesting disagreement.

When the cooperative doubled in size, a treasurer proposed that one night on watch earn one credit. Anyone who had used up her credits would take the next available shift. The proposal appealed especially to newcomers. An established potter could decline a night with a two-word reference to a sick aunt. A newcomer with an equally sick relative might have to tell a long and embarrassing story before the request seemed reasonable. A credit in the book would entitle either to say no without giving an account of her household. It would be easy to mistake the old members' discretion for a courtesy that the new members enjoyed equally.

After a season of bookkeeping, however, two experienced members objected that the accounts omitted the work of instructing novices. Teaching someone to load the kiln might save the cooperative many spoiled firings, yet no credit was issued for it. The treasurer offered to add a column for instruction. This reply pleased the member who did most of the teaching. It failed to satisfy the other, who had never taught a novice. Her complaint was that the new arrangement settled in advance which acts the members could invoke when deciding a shift. Before the ledger, she said, a contribution that nobody had thought important on Monday could be recognized as decisive on Friday. With another column there would merely be two things the cooperative had already thought of on Monday.

The distinction is easy to miss if we ask members only whether they consider the distribution of nights fair. Both critics might give the same low rating, and the newcomer, glad of her credit, a high one. If the credit for teaching were introduced, a rise in the average rating could be perfectly genuine without answering the second critic. Her concern would be better tested by watching what happens the first time a member offers a reason for changing shifts that the ledger has no place to record.

Nothing in this account requires the cooperative to abandon credits. A member who can politely decline without describing an ill relative has gained something that a richer communal discussion would not supply. The choice worth investigating is whether a posted balance must settle every case, or whether a member may occasionally reopen a case without being forced to reopen the door to her private life.

Why distinguish the critic who teaches from the critic who does not?
Choices:
To suggest that only a person who teaches can judge the value of instruction
To show why the fairness ratings of the two critics would necessarily differ
To establish that opposition to credits originated among the newest members
To show how the same omitted activity can reveal two different objections to the ledger
Answer: To show how the same omitted activity can reveal two different objections to the ledger
Reason: One critic wants an existing contribution counted. The other objects to deciding beforehand what can count.

Topic: CARS · Social sciences · Counting library requests
Prompt:
Every spring our library association prints a league table of the most requested books. The figures are exact enough. A borrower enters a title on a slip, hands it to the clerk, and the clerk records one request. Last year a trustee proposed that the association buy next year's books in proportion to the totals on those slips. A branch serving keen readers of gardening books would acquire more gardening books. A branch whose readers cared little for gardening would be spared them. The proposal sounded like a modest way of letting readers themselves write the purchase order.

I spent a morning beside the returns counter at two branches. At the first, the clerk knew that three copies of a popular garden manual had recently arrived. She pointed people toward a shelf so close to the counter that she could see the green covers from her chair. At the second branch a reader looking for that manual was told that the only copy had gone missing. He filled in a slip. By noon the first branch had put the manual into six hands and registered no requests for it. The second had registered four requests and put the book into no hands at all.

The trustee had made a reasonable inference from a different sort of record. If people unable to borrow a book invariably filled in a slip, four slips would indeed mark four occasions on which another copy might have helped. She had quietly extended that inference to a comparison of readers' interests across branches. Yet the success that a well-stocked branch enjoyed in meeting an interest also gave that interest a way to disappear from the list. One could buy exactly in proportion to the figures and, a year later, congratulate oneself on having reduced the recorded enthusiasm for precisely the books the new copies were serving.

There is a more uncomfortable complication. At a third branch the slips sit behind the counter. The clerk gladly provides one to anyone who asks. A reader first has to know that the little transaction is possible, then care enough to conduct it in front of three people waiting to borrow books. Moving the slips out onto a table might increase requests while leaving both the collection and the readers' wishes unchanged. That rise would be an achievement for the new arrangement. It would be a curious reason to charge the branch with a sudden failure to stock its shelves.

I would keep the figures. On a particular afternoon four unsuccessful searches for the same manual give a librarian a fine reason to telephone another branch. When deciding how to spend next year's money, I would ask the successful readers a question too. The slip was designed to help someone who had gone away empty-handed. Its designers deserve credit for recording a disappointment so that someone could act on it. They never arranged to count every occasion for delight.

Which claim best expresses the author's objection to proportional purchasing?
Choices:
The meaning of a request count depends on how books and request slips are made available.
Clerks cannot reliably remember which titles borrowers have requested.
The association should give branches equal budgets regardless of their readers.
Purchases should follow the number of visitors rather than any record of reading.
Answer: The meaning of a request count depends on how books and request slips are made available.
Reason: The two branch comparisons show how both supply and ease of reporting affect what gets counted.

Topic: CARS · Humanities · Sitting for a portrait
Prompt:
For the first hour of sitting for my portrait, I tried to hold a pleasant expression that I imagined I wore whenever I opened the door to a friend. The painter let me keep it until the effort began to show. Then she asked me to describe the walk to her studio. She put down the little brush with which she had been drawing my mouth and picked up a larger one.

It is tempting to give the painter an easy victory here. Say that the camera copies surfaces while the painter sees a person, and the case is closed. A convincing likeness can emerge when a chosen feature meets a viewer's experience of the sitter.

Prompt: What comparison is missing if a patient hears only about the recommended intervention?
Answer: Reasonable alternatives, including forgoing treatment and its likely consequences.
Reason: The patient needs a reference point for the proposed benefit and harm.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Informed consent · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/informed-consent

Topic: Comparing a proposed intervention with observation or deferral
Prompt: A stable patient asks what happens if they choose monitoring for a condition that can safely be observed. What should the clinician explain?
Answer: The expected course with observation and what change would prompt reassessment.
Reason: Observation can be an active option with a follow-up plan.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Informed consent · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/informed-consent

Topic: Comparing a proposed intervention with observation or deferral
Prompt: A patient with a time-sensitive condition asks whether waiting is an option. What should the clinician disclose about waiting?
Answer: The risks of delay, including loss of benefit if a treatment window closes.
Reason: Respecting choice includes explaining time-sensitive consequences.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Informed consent · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/informed-consent

Topic: Comparing a proposed intervention with observation or deferral
Prompt: When active surveillance is offered alongside treatment, what practical requirement should be made explicit?
Answer: What monitoring is needed and when a change would prompt treatment.
Reason: Surveillance involves continued assessment.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Informed consent · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/informed-consent

Topic: Comparing a proposed intervention with observation or deferral
Prompt: A patient prefers surveillance but thinks this means no further visits or tests. What is the most important misconception to correct?
Answer: Explain the required follow-up and the findings that would trigger reconsideration.
Reason: The choice should reflect what the strategy actually involves.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Informed consent · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/informed-consent

Topic: Comparing a proposed intervention with observation or deferral
Prompt: A patient understands surveillance but cannot travel for the required visits. What should the team explore before finalizing that choice?
Answer: Whether monitoring can be made accessible or another reasonable option would fit better.
Reason: Feasibility changes the choice even if the biological risks are unchanged.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Informed consent · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/informed-consent

Topic: Comparing a proposed intervention with observation or deferral
Prompt: What should a clinician clarify after a capable patient declines one proposed intervention?
Answer: Which other forms of care the patient would still accept.
Reason: Refusal can be specific to one intervention.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Informed consent · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/informed-consent

Topic: Comparing a proposed intervention with observation or deferral
Prompt: A patient declines elective surgery but wants help managing pain. What care should remain available?
Answer: Discuss and offer appropriate symptom treatment and follow-up.
Reason: Declining surgery does not end the therapeutic relationship.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Informed consent · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/informed-consent

Topic: Comparing a proposed intervention with observation or deferral
Prompt: A patient who once declined surgery now asks to reconsider after symptoms worsen. What should the clinician do?
Answer: Reassess current options and revisit the informed decision with the patient.
Reason: A prior capable refusal does not permanently bind a capable patient who changes their mind.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Informed consent · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/informed-consent

Topic: Consent and interpretation when a placebo is proposed
Prompt: What makes a substance a placebo for the specific condition being treated?
Answer: It has no expected specific pharmacologic effect on that condition.
Reason: Context and expectations can still affect the patient's experience.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Use of placebo in clinical practice · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/use-placebo-clinical-practice

Topic: Consent and interpretation when a placebo is proposed
Prompt: A patient who agreed to a placebo reports less pain after taking it. Does that response show the original pain was fabricated?
Answer: No. Symptom improvement does not establish deception.
Reason: A placebo response cannot separate genuine from feigned pain.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Use of placebo in clinical practice · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/use-placebo-clinical-practice

Topic: Consent and interpretation when a placebo is proposed
Prompt: A patient reports no relief after an agreed placebo. Does this prove the symptom has a specific organic cause?
Answer: No. Lack of a placebo response does not determine etiology.
Reason: Investigate according to the clinical history and findings.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Use of placebo in clinical practice · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/use-placebo-clinical-practice

Topic: Consent and interpretation when a placebo is proposed
Prompt: For placebo use compatible with good clinical care, what does the AMA say the patient must generally agree to?
Answer: The possibility of receiving a placebo.
Reason: Consent need not specify exactly when a placebo will be used.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Use of placebo in clinical practice · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/use-placebo-clinical-practice

Topic: Consent and interpretation when a placebo is proposed
Prompt: An informed patient explicitly agrees that an appropriate trial may include placebo at an unspecified point. Is the undisclosed timing alone a violation of that agreement?
Answer: No. The timing can remain unspecified within the patient's agreed plan.
Reason: The possible use of placebo was discussed.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Use of placebo in clinical practice · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/use-placebo-clinical-practice

Topic: Consent and interpretation when a placebo is proposed
Prompt: A patient declines the physician's proposal to include a placebo in symptom treatment. What should the physician do?
Answer: Respect the refusal and discuss other appropriate measures.
Reason: Avoid covert substitution.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Use of placebo in clinical practice · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/use-placebo-clinical-practice

Topic: Consent and interpretation when a placebo is proposed
Prompt: A patient originally agreed to possible placebo use but now withdraws that permission while still requesting treatment. What changes?
Answer: Stop placebo use and revise the care plan with the patient.
Reason: The previous agreement does not authorize continued use after withdrawal.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Use of placebo in clinical practice · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/use-placebo-clinical-practice

Topic: Managing financial interests in clinical recommendations
Prompt: A physician earns more if patients choose a facility she partly owns. Which feature creates a conflict even when the test is indicated?
Answer: The physician's financial interest in the destination of the referral.
Reason: A sound indication does not remove the competing interest.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Physician self-referral · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/physician-self-referral

Topic: Managing financial interests in clinical recommendations
Prompt: A physician with no stake in a facility recommends it because it is the only center offering a needed service. Does this fact alone show a financial self-referral conflict?
Answer: No financial interest is identified in this scenario.
Reason: Evaluate the actual relationship and alternatives.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Physician self-referral · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/physician-self-referral

Topic: Managing financial interests in clinical recommendations
Prompt: What information helps a patient evaluate a referral to a clinician-owned facility?
Answer: The clinician's interest and reasonable alternative providers when available.
Reason: This supports an informed choice about where to receive a needed service.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Physician self-referral · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/physician-self-referral

Topic: Managing financial interests in clinical recommendations
Prompt: After hearing the ownership disclosure, a patient requests a medically appropriate independent imaging center. What should the referring physician do?
Answer: Facilitate the patient's informed choice of provider.
Reason: Disclosure is meaningful only if the patient can act on it.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Physician self-referral · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/physician-self-referral

Topic: Managing financial interests in clinical recommendations
Prompt: Which judgment should precede a discussion of where a patient will receive a profitable service?
Answer: Whether the service is medically appropriate for this patient.
Reason: A financial benefit must not drive the indication.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Physician self-referral · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/physician-self-referral

Topic: Managing financial interests in clinical recommendations
Prompt: A test is clinically indicated and a physician-owned site is a reasonable option. What does the patient need before selecting it?
Answer: Disclosure of the interest and a fair discussion of reasonable alternatives.
Reason: The patient can then choose where to obtain appropriate care.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Physician self-referral · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/physician-self-referral

Topic: Including children in treatment decisions at their developmental level
Prompt: A ten-year-old understands an elective procedure when it is explained simply, but nobody has spoken to them. What should the clinician seek in addition to parental permission?
Reason: Speak directly to the child and invite questions.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Pediatric decision making · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/pediatric-decision-making

Topic: Including children in treatment decisions at their developmental level
Prompt: A toddler cannot weigh treatment options but can choose which arm to offer for a routine examination. How can the clinician include the child?
Answer: Offer the manageable choice while the authorized adult provides permission for care.
Reason: Participation can match the child's abilities.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Pediatric decision making · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/pediatric-decision-making

Topic: Including children in treatment decisions at their developmental level
Prompt: What should the clinician first try to understand when a child resists a proposed intervention?
Answer: The reason for the resistance and the child's understanding of the intervention.
Reason: Pain, fear and misunderstood consequences invite different responses.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Pediatric decision making · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/pediatric-decision-making

Topic: Including children in treatment decisions at their developmental level
Prompt: A child resists an immediately necessary treatment because of needle fear. A parent authorizes it and delay risks serious harm. How should the team handle the fear?
Answer: Address distress and proceed with the necessary care using appropriate comfort measures.
Reason: Urgency changes whether assent can be awaited.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Pediatric decision making · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/pediatric-decision-making

Topic: Including children in treatment decisions at their developmental level
Prompt: What makes deferring an intervention especially reasonable when a mature adolescent objects?
Answer: The intervention can safely wait without sacrificing substantial benefit.
Reason: Use the time to understand dissent and discuss alternatives.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Pediatric decision making · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/pediatric-decision-making

Topic: Including children in treatment decisions at their developmental level
Prompt: Parents decline urgently necessary treatment and the team believes the delay places a child at serious imminent risk. What escalation should accompany efforts to reach agreement?
Answer: Activate the institution's urgent ethics and protective or legal pathway under applicable law.
Reason: The emergency team must act in time to protect the child.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Pediatric decision making · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/pediatric-decision-making

Topic: Assessing understanding, appreciation and reasoning for a specific choice
Prompt: What does appreciation mean in a decision-specific capacity assessment?
Answer: Recognizing how the condition and likely consequences apply to oneself.
Reason: Repeating general facts demonstrates a different ability.
Source: Paul S. Appelbaum · Assessment of patients' competence to consent to treatment · https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMcp074045

Topic: Assessing understanding, appreciation and reasoning for a specific choice
Prompt: A patient says, “I know this could kill me soon, but the treatment burden is more than I want.” Does that statement by itself demonstrate impaired appreciation?
Answer: No. It shows recognition that the risk can apply personally.
Reason: Assess the other abilities and voluntariness.
Source: Paul S. Appelbaum · Assessment of patients' competence to consent to treatment · https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMcp074045

Topic: Assessing understanding, appreciation and reasoning for a specific choice
Prompt: What practical step should precede a judgment of incapacity when a patient appears unable to follow the discussion?
Answer: Correct reversible communication barriers and explain the decision accessibly.
Reason: Assess what the patient can do with appropriate support.
Source: Paul S. Appelbaum · Assessment of patients' competence to consent to treatment · https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMcp074045

Topic: Responding to an informed refusal without abandoning the patient
Prompt: What gives a capable adult's refusal of a recommended treatment ethical authority?
Answer: A voluntary, informed choice about their own care.
Reason: Explore understanding and reasons without coercion.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Informed consent · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/informed-consent

Topic: Responding to an informed refusal without abandoning the patient
Prompt: A patient declines a diagnostic ultrasound solely because they believe it involves ionizing radiation. What should the clinician do before concluding that the refusal is informed?
Answer: Correct the misconception and invite the patient to reconsider or reaffirm the choice.
Reason: The patient's decision still governs once they understand.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Informed consent · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/informed-consent

Topic: Responding to an informed refusal without abandoning the patient
Prompt: What should the clinician clarify when a patient says, “I don't want that treatment”?
Answer: Which part they decline and why.
Reason: The patient may object to a burden, misunderstand a risk, or lack access.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Informed consent · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/informed-consent

Topic: Responding to an informed refusal without abandoning the patient
Prompt: A patient rejects a proposed operation but requests treatment that can relieve symptoms without surgery. What should the clinician discuss?
Answer: Reasonable nonsurgical options and their expected outcomes.
Reason: The refusal applies to surgery.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Informed consent · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/informed-consent

Topic: Responding to an informed refusal without abandoning the patient
Prompt: A patient recorded as “refusing treatment” explains that they want it but cannot reach the clinic. What should the team address?
Answer: The access barrier and feasible ways to receive care.
Reason: Preference for treatment was obscured by a practical obstacle.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Informed consent · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/informed-consent

Topic: Responding to an informed refusal without abandoning the patient
Prompt: A capable adult understands the risks of declining a proposed procedure and confirms the choice. What should the clinician document about the discussion?
Answer: The particular refusal, the information and alternatives discussed, the patient's understanding and follow-up plan.
Reason: Document the patient's own reasoning where possible.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Informed consent · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/informed-consent

Topic: Preventing and responding to a retained surgical item
Prompt: Why can an apparently correct surgical count fail to exclude an unintentionally retained item?
Answer: The starting or final inventory may itself be wrong.
Reason: Counting and methodical wound exploration provide complementary checks.
Source: American College of Surgeons · Prevention of unintentionally retained surgical items · https://www.facs.org/about-acs/statements/prevention-of-unintentionally-retained-surgical-items-after-surgery/

Topic: Preventing and responding to a retained surgical item
Prompt: The closing record shows the team opened two sponge packs. Compare the expected and recovered counts in the record. How many sponges are unaccounted for?
Reason: Fifteen were introduced and fourteen recovered. The discrepancy requires immediate reconciliation.
Source: American College of Surgeons · Prevention of unintentionally retained surgical items · https://www.facs.org/about-acs/statements/prevention-of-unintentionally-retained-surgical-items-after-surgery/

Topic: Preventing and responding to a retained surgical item
Prompt: The tally in this record balances, but a team member reports seeing a sponge deep in the wound after the count. What finding must still be investigated before routine closure?
Answer: The direct report of a possible retained sponge.
Reason: A balanced count cannot override independent contrary evidence.
Source: American College of Surgeons · Prevention of unintentionally retained surgical items · https://www.facs.org/about-acs/statements/prevention-of-unintentionally-retained-surgical-items-after-surgery/

Topic: Preventing and responding to a retained surgical item
Prompt: What should the team do immediately when a closing surgical count is discrepant in a stable patient?
Answer: Tell the operating team and pause routine closure for reconciliation.
Reason: Use the institutional search, repeat-count and imaging protocol as indicated.
Source: American College of Surgeons · Prevention of unintentionally retained surgical items · https://www.facs.org/about-acs/statements/prevention-of-unintentionally-retained-surgical-items-after-surgery/

Topic: Preventing and responding to a retained surgical item
Prompt: A stable patient's team cannot locate a missing radiopaque sponge after a recount and methodical search. What additional check should be considered under the count-discrepancy protocol?
Answer: Appropriate intraoperative imaging before the patient leaves the operating room.
Reason: Inform those interpreting the image exactly what is missing.
Source: American College of Surgeons · Prevention of unintentionally retained surgical items · https://www.facs.org/about-acs/statements/prevention-of-unintentionally-retained-surgical-items-after-surgery/

Topic: Preventing and responding to a retained surgical item
Prompt: A missing sponge is found in the waste during the search. What should be verified before calling the count resolved?
Answer: Correctly identify it, repeat and reconcile the count, and document the resolution.
Reason: Finding an object requires confirmation against the actual discrepancy.
Source: American College of Surgeons · Prevention of unintentionally retained surgical items · https://www.facs.org/about-acs/statements/prevention-of-unintentionally-retained-surgical-items-after-surgery/

Topic: Preventing and responding to a retained surgical item
Prompt: What information should travel with a patient when packing is intentionally left during staged surgery?
Answer: What was left, where, and who will remove it and when.
Reason: Document and communicate the plan directly.
Source: American College of Surgeons · Prevention of unintentionally retained surgical items · https://www.facs.org/about-acs/statements/prevention-of-unintentionally-retained-surgical-items-after-surgery/

Topic: Preventing and responding to a retained surgical item
Prompt: After emergency surgery, the handoff says only “packing left.” What should the receiving team clarify with the operating team?
Answer: The type, amount and location of packing and the explicit removal plan.
Reason: Intentional packing needs a traceable plan across teams.
Source: American College of Surgeons · Prevention of unintentionally retained surgical items · https://www.facs.org/about-acs/statements/prevention-of-unintentionally-retained-surgical-items-after-surgery/

Topic: Preventing and responding to a retained surgical item
Prompt: An unexpected radiopaque sponge marker is reported after surgery and there was no plan to leave packing. What should the responsible clinician do first?
Answer: Promptly assess the patient and notify the operating team to investigate and arrange management.
Reason: A previously correct count does not resolve the new clinical finding.
Source: American College of Surgeons · Prevention of unintentionally retained surgical items · https://www.facs.org/about-acs/statements/prevention-of-unintentionally-retained-surgical-items-after-surgery/

Topic: Reconciling identity, site and procedure before incision
Prompt: Just before incision the surgeon silently reviews the consent while other staff are still setting up. Which safety step remains incomplete?
Answer: An active time-out involving the immediate procedure team.
Reason: The check requires shared agreement on patient, procedure and site.
Source: The Joint Commission · Universal Protocol · https://www.jointcommission.org/-/media/tjc/documents/standards/universal-protocol/up_poster1pdf.pdf

Topic: Reconciling identity, site and procedure before incision
Prompt: The preprocedure assessment was completed in clinic yesterday. What final verification is still needed in the operating room?
Answer: A team time-out immediately before starting the procedure.
Reason: Earlier verification and the point-of-procedure check serve different purposes.
Source: The Joint Commission · Universal Protocol · https://www.jointcommission.org/-/media/tjc/documents/standards/universal-protocol/up_poster1pdf.pdf

Topic: Reconciling identity, site and procedure before incision
Prompt: What should happen if a discrepancy remains after preprocedure verification?
Answer: Pause until the team resolves it using reliable information.
Reason: Do not infer the answer from the schedule alone.
Source: The Joint Commission · Universal Protocol · https://www.jointcommission.org/-/media/tjc/documents/standards/universal-protocol/up_poster1pdf.pdf

Topic: Reconciling identity, site and procedure before incision
Prompt: The patient and site mark agree on the right knee, but the schedule lists reconstruction while the signed consent and patient describe diagnostic arthroscopy. What should happen before incision?
Answer: Stop and reconcile the intended procedure and consent with the patient and team.
Reason: Agreement on laterality leaves the procedure discrepancy unresolved.
Source: The Joint Commission · Universal Protocol · https://www.jointcommission.org/-/media/tjc/documents/standards/universal-protocol/up_poster1pdf.pdf

Topic: Reconciling identity, site and procedure before incision
Prompt: What is the team's obligation when anyone identifies an unresolved mismatch during the final time-out?
Answer: Stop progression and resolve the concern before starting.
Reason: Role or seniority does not determine whether a concern counts.
Source: The Joint Commission · Universal Protocol · https://www.jointcommission.org/-/media/tjc/documents/standards/universal-protocol/up_poster1pdf.pdf

Topic: Reconciling identity, site and procedure before incision
Prompt: During one anesthetic, a different surgeon takes over to perform a second invasive procedure. What verification is required before the second procedure starts?
Answer: Conduct another time-out with the immediate procedure team.
Reason: The change in proceduralist for a separate procedure requires its own verification.
Source: The Joint Commission · Universal Protocol · https://www.jointcommission.org/-/media/tjc/documents/standards/universal-protocol/up_poster1pdf.pdf

Topic: Communicating confirmed facts and following up after harm
Prompt: A patient asks why the infusion was given too quickly. The team knows the rate delivered but has not determined the cause. What should the clinician say about the cause?
Answer: Acknowledge that the cause is still being investigated and arrange an update.
Reason: Share the known facts and effects now without guessing.
Source: AHRQ · CANDOR response and disclosure · https://www.ahrq.gov/patient-safety/settings/hospital/candor/modules/guide5/notes.html

Topic: Communicating confirmed facts and following up after harm
Prompt: A review confirms that a dose was ten times the order. The contributing system failures remain uncertain. Which fact can be stated plainly now?
Answer: The patient received ten times the ordered dose.
Reason: Uncertainty about why the error occurred does not erase what has been verified.
Source: AHRQ · CANDOR response and disclosure · https://www.ahrq.gov/patient-safety/settings/hospital/candor/modules/guide5/notes.html

Topic: Communicating confirmed facts and following up after harm
Prompt: Which immediate patient need comes before assembling a complete explanation of a harmful event?
Answer: Assessing and treating any ongoing clinical harm.
Reason: Disclosure and investigation proceed alongside clinical care.
Source: AHRQ · CANDOR response and disclosure · https://www.ahrq.gov/patient-safety/settings/hospital/candor/modules/guide5/notes.html

Topic: Communicating confirmed facts and following up after harm
Prompt: During disclosure a patient interrupts, “Am I still in danger right now?” What should the clinician address next?
Answer: Explain the patient's current condition, immediate risks and treatment plan in plain language.
Reason: Return to the remaining facts and questions after addressing the patient's priority.
Source: AHRQ · CANDOR response and disclosure · https://www.ahrq.gov/patient-safety/settings/hospital/candor/modules/guide5/notes.html

Topic: Communicating confirmed facts and following up after harm
Prompt: What should the initial disclosure establish about communication after a harmful event?
Answer: Who will contact the patient again, how and when.
Reason: Give the patient a point of contact for new questions.
Source: AHRQ · CANDOR response and disclosure · https://www.ahrq.gov/patient-safety/settings/hospital/candor/modules/guide5/notes.html

Topic: Communicating confirmed facts and following up after harm
Prompt: The agreed update day arrives and the investigation remains open. What should the named clinician do?
Answer: Contact the patient as promised, share what is known and agree on the next update.
Reason: An unfinished investigation should not create unexplained silence.
Source: AHRQ · CANDOR response and disclosure · https://www.ahrq.gov/patient-safety/settings/hospital/candor/modules/guide5/notes.html

Topic: Preventing ambiguous and wrong-chart medication orders
Prompt: What is the danger of omitting the leading zero from a decimal dose such as .5 mg?
Answer: A missed decimal point can turn the intended dose into 5 mg.
Reason: Write 0.5 mg. Avoid trailing zeros for whole-number doses.
Source: ISMP · Error-prone abbreviations, symbols and dose designations · https://www.ismp.org/system/files/resources/2024-04/ISMP_ErrorProneAbbreviation_List.pdf

Topic: Preventing ambiguous and wrong-chart medication orders
Prompt: A medication order reads “5.0 mg.” Which safer notation preserves the intended quantity?
Reason: A trailing zero can create a tenfold error if the decimal is overlooked.
Source: ISMP · Error-prone abbreviations, symbols and dose designations · https://www.ismp.org/system/files/resources/2024-04/ISMP_ErrorProneAbbreviation_List.pdf

Topic: Preventing ambiguous and wrong-chart medication orders
Prompt: The signed order clearly specifies 5 mg but the label on the dispensed syringe states 50 mg. At which stage is the first documented discrepancy?
Answer: Dispensing or preparation after the order.
Reason: Changing how the original prescriber writes 5 mg would not resolve this mismatch.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Computerized provider order entry · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/computerized-provider-order-entry

Topic: Preventing ambiguous and wrong-chart medication orders
Prompt: Which check is most directly relevant before signing an order after switching patient charts?
Answer: Actively confirm patient-specific identifiers against the intended patient.
Reason: A familiar name or room can give false reassurance.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Computerized provider order entry · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/computerized-provider-order-entry

Topic: Preventing ambiguous and wrong-chart medication orders
Prompt: The patient identifiers match, but a newly entered dose differs tenfold from the documented plan. What should the team do before administration?
Answer: Clarify the intended dose with the prescriber and correct the order if needed.
Reason: Identity verification cannot resolve a dose discrepancy.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Computerized provider order entry · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/computerized-provider-order-entry

Topic: Preventing ambiguous and wrong-chart medication orders
Prompt: What should the team establish promptly after discovering a wrong medication order?
Answer: Whether it reached dispensing or administration and whether the patient was exposed.
Reason: Existing downstream copies can persist after the order is changed.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Computerized provider order entry · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/computerized-provider-order-entry

Topic: Preventing ambiguous and wrong-chart medication orders
Prompt: A wrong-chart order is found before the dose is given. It already appears on the nursing worklist. What communication is needed in addition to cancellation?
Answer: Notify the administering team, confirm the dose is withheld and verify that the active worklist is corrected.
Reason: Changing a narrative note alone leaves an actionable order in circulation.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Computerized provider order entry · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/computerized-provider-order-entry

Topic: Preventing ambiguous and wrong-chart medication orders
Prompt: A wrong-chart order is discovered after a dose was given. What is the immediate clinical priority?
Answer: Assess the exposed patient and manage possible harm.
Reason: Then correct orders and follow disclosure and reporting procedures.
Source: AHRQ · CANDOR response and disclosure · https://www.ahrq.gov/patient-safety/settings/hospital/candor/modules/guide5/notes.html

Topic: Matching the supplied medication to the prescription
Prompt: What does the dispensing check compare with the original prescription?
Answer: The actual medication, strength, dosage form, label and intended patient.
Reason: A correct printed label can be attached to an incorrect product.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Medication errors in retail pharmacies · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/web-mm/medication-errors-retail-pharmacies-wrong-patient-wrong-instructions

Topic: Matching the supplied medication to the prescription
Prompt: The record shows that a prescribed immediate-release product was filled with an extended-release product of the same strength. Which property was mismatched?
Reason: Matching the drug name and milligrams cannot establish interchangeability.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Medication errors in retail pharmacies · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/web-mm/medication-errors-retail-pharmacies-wrong-patient-wrong-instructions

Topic: Matching the supplied medication to the prescription
Prompt: The order and dispensed drug name and formulation agree in the record. What remaining discrepancy needs correction?
Answer: The dispensed tablet strength is twice the prescribed strength.
Reason: A correct drug and formulation can still deliver the wrong dose.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Medication errors in retail pharmacies · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/web-mm/medication-errors-retail-pharmacies-wrong-patient-wrong-instructions

Topic: Matching the supplied medication to the prescription
Prompt: What should a pharmacist verify when a patient questions an unfamiliar tablet at pickup?
Answer: Compare the actual product and identifiers against the verified prescription and label.
Reason: Appearance alone cannot determine whether it is the correct medicine.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Medication errors in retail pharmacies · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/web-mm/medication-errors-retail-pharmacies-wrong-patient-wrong-instructions
