Prompt: A team finds the same routine check performed four different ways with no clinical reason for variation. What initial design change is reasonable?
Answer: Agree on a standard, evidence-informed method and pilot it with the users.
Reason: Measure performance and unintended consequences.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Separating unwarranted variation from appropriate individualization
Prompt: A default medication on a pathway is contraindicated for one patient. What should the team do with the pathway in this case?
Answer: Use and document the appropriate exception, then ensure a safe alternative plan.
Reason: A high compliance target cannot justify an unsafe default.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Using checklists to surface unresolved concerns
Prompt: What is the purpose of verbally confirming key checks as a procedure team?
Answer: To share relevant information and identify unresolved discrepancies before harm.
Reason: Completing a form is one aid to this process.
Source: WHO · Surgical safety checklist implementation manual · https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241598590

Topic: Using checklists to surface unresolved concerns
Prompt: A coordinator fills in every team time-out box before anyone enters the room. What is missing?
Answer: Actual confirmation by the participating team at the appropriate time.
Reason: A prefilled record does not demonstrate performance.
Source: WHO · Surgical safety checklist implementation manual · https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241598590

Topic: Using checklists to surface unresolved concerns
Prompt: At the time-out the team discovers a side discrepancy and postpones incision. Did the checklist process fail merely because it delayed starting?
Answer: No. Detecting the discrepancy before incision is an intended function.
Reason: Resolve the concern before proceeding.
Source: WHO · Surgical safety checklist implementation manual · https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241598590

Topic: Using checklists to surface unresolved concerns
Prompt: What comparison separates a missing checklist safeguard from a skipped one?
Answer: Compare the written checklist with observation of how it was actually used.
Reason: The remedies address different causes.
Source: WHO · Surgical safety checklist implementation manual · https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241598590

Topic: Using checklists to surface unresolved concerns
Prompt: A team faithfully completes the full checklist, but the local high-risk step identified in repeated incidents is absent. What needs review?
Answer: The checklist's content and fit to the local workflow.
Reason: Pilot a change based on the identified hazard.
Source: WHO · Surgical safety checklist implementation manual · https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241598590

Topic: Using checklists to surface unresolved concerns
Prompt: The required check is present in the checklist, but auditors see staff prefill it before the information arrives. What needs review?
Answer: How and when the team executes the check.
Reason: Adding the same words a second time is unlikely to fix the workflow.
Source: WHO · Surgical safety checklist implementation manual · https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241598590

Topic: Using checklists to surface unresolved concerns
Prompt: What observation helps validate a reported 100% checklist completion rate?
Answer: Direct observation of whether the checks occur at the intended time with the relevant team.
Reason: Paper completion and meaningful execution can diverge.
Source: WHO · Surgical safety checklist implementation manual · https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241598590

Topic: Using checklists to surface unresolved concerns
Prompt: A surgical checklist pilot finds introductions and hazard discussion occur in only half of directly observed cases despite signed forms. Which behavior should the next test target?
Answer: The team's actual participation in the discussion.
Reason: Engage users to identify barriers and remeasure observed execution.
Source: WHO · Surgical safety checklist implementation manual · https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241598590

Topic: Using checklists to surface unresolved concerns
Prompt: The next pilot produces high observed participation. What additional evidence should be followed before declaring the risk controlled?
Answer: Whether discrepancies are detected and resolved and whether targeted harms or delays change.
Reason: Execution is necessary but does not by itself establish outcome improvement.
Source: WHO · Surgical safety checklist implementation manual · https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241598590

Topic: Defining the eligible denominator and unit of analysis
Prompt: If an improvement aim concerns the proportion of unique patients reached, what is the counting unit?
Reason: Define how repeat encounters are handled.
Source: CMS · Developing measure specifications · https://mmshub-impl.cms.gov/measure-lifecycle/measure-specification/develop-specification/overview

Topic: Defining the eligible denominator and unit of analysis
Prompt: A clinic records 60 completed calls to 40 different patients among 100 eligible patients. What fraction of eligible patients was reached?
Reason: The numerator is unique patients reached, not calls completed.
Source: CMS · Developing measure specifications · https://mmshub-impl.cms.gov/measure-lifecycle/measure-specification/develop-specification/overview

Topic: Defining the eligible denominator and unit of analysis
Prompt: A different measure asks what fraction of 80 attempted calls connected, and 60 connected. What is the success rate per attempt?
Reason: The denominator is attempts because the question concerns calls.
Source: CMS · Developing measure specifications · https://mmshub-impl.cms.gov/measure-lifecycle/measure-specification/develop-specification/overview

Topic: Defining the eligible denominator and unit of analysis
Prompt: What information is missing from a simple count of device-associated events when comparing units?
Answer: How much time patients were exposed to the device.
Reason: A device-day denominator accounts for exposure opportunity.
Source: CMS · Developing measure specifications · https://mmshub-impl.cms.gov/measure-lifecycle/measure-specification/develop-specification/overview

Topic: Defining the eligible denominator and unit of analysis
Prompt: Two units each report 4 central-line infections. One has 500 line-days, the other 1,000. Which has the higher observed rate per 1,000 line-days?
Answer: The 500-line-day unit, at 8 rather than 4 per 1,000.
Reason: Compare counts divided by exposure over the same period.
Source: CMS · Developing measure specifications · https://mmshub-impl.cms.gov/measure-lifecycle/measure-specification/develop-specification/overview

Topic: Defining the eligible denominator and unit of analysis
Prompt: What should be documented before a performance measure is tracked over time?
Answer: Its numerator, denominator, exclusions, interval and data source.
Reason: These specifications make repeated measurements comparable.
Source: CMS · Developing measure specifications · https://mmshub-impl.cms.gov/measure-lifecycle/measure-specification/develop-specification/overview

Topic: Defining the eligible denominator and unit of analysis
Prompt: A policy expands eligibility for screening to a new age group midyear. How could the clinic compare delivery over time without hiding that change?
Answer: Report the originally eligible group consistently and report the newly eligible group separately, or establish a clearly labeled new baseline.
Reason: A changed population can shift a rate without changing delivery.
Source: CMS · Developing measure specifications · https://mmshub-impl.cms.gov/measure-lifecycle/measure-specification/develop-specification/overview

Topic: Applying published measure specifications before comparing clinicians
Prompt: What does a quality measure specification define for participating clinicians?
Answer: Exactly what is measured, including the eligible population and how performance is counted.
Reason: The definition allows comparable reporting.
Source: CMS · Developing measure specifications · https://mmshub-impl.cms.gov/measure-lifecycle/measure-specification/develop-specification/overview

Topic: Applying published measure specifications before comparing clinicians
Prompt: A process measure includes adults treated during the year and excludes a specified contraindication. A patient's documented contraindication meets that exclusion. Where does that patient belong in the reported eligible denominator?
Answer: Outside the denominator under that specification.
Reason: Apply the published rule, not an improvised exclusion.
Source: CMS · Developing measure specifications · https://mmshub-impl.cms.gov/measure-lifecycle/measure-specification/develop-specification/overview

Topic: Applying published measure specifications before comparing clinicians
Prompt: A clinician feels a patient was atypical, but the patient meets eligibility and no published exclusion or exception applies. May the reviewer quietly remove that patient to improve the score?
Answer: No. Apply the specification consistently and flag any limitation separately.
Reason: Discretionary exclusions undermine comparability.
Source: CMS · Developing measure specifications · https://mmshub-impl.cms.gov/measure-lifecycle/measure-specification/develop-specification/overview

Topic: Applying published measure specifications before comparing clinicians
Prompt: What should accompany a clinician's count of patients meeting a process measure?
Answer: The number of eligible patients and the measure period.
Reason: Include exclusions as defined by the specification.
Source: CMS · Developing measure specifications · https://mmshub-impl.cms.gov/measure-lifecycle/measure-specification/develop-specification/overview

Topic: Applying published measure specifications before comparing clinicians
Prompt: Review the two clinicians' reports. Which clinician had the higher proportion meeting the process measure?
Reason: A delivered the service to 48 of 60 (80%); B delivered it to 27 of 30 (90%).
Source: CMS · Developing measure specifications · https://mmshub-impl.cms.gov/measure-lifecycle/measure-specification/develop-specification/overview

Topic: Applying published measure specifications before comparing clinicians
Prompt: A clinician meets a measure for 4 of 4 eligible patients. What important limitation applies to treating that 100% as a stable ranking?
Answer: The estimate is based on very few eligible cases.
Reason: One additional case can change the percentage substantially.
Source: CMS · Developing measure specifications · https://mmshub-impl.cms.gov/measure-lifecycle/measure-specification/develop-specification/overview

Topic: Applying published measure specifications before comparing clinicians
Prompt: What should a practice verify when a reported quality score changes sharply at a reporting-year boundary?
Answer: Whether measure definitions, data capture or patient eligibility changed.
Reason: Inspect underlying cases before attributing the change to care.
Source: CMS · Developing measure specifications · https://mmshub-impl.cms.gov/measure-lifecycle/measure-specification/develop-specification/overview

Topic: Applying published measure specifications before comparing clinicians
Prompt: The new measure version changes the follow-up window from 30 to 60 days. Can the new score be directly interpreted against the old 30-day trend?
Answer: No. Recompute using a common window or clearly mark a new series.
Reason: The outcome has more time in which to occur.
Source: CMS · Developing measure specifications · https://mmshub-impl.cms.gov/measure-lifecycle/measure-specification/develop-specification/overview

Topic: Applying published measure specifications before comparing clinicians
Prompt: The measure specification is unchanged, but completed services disappeared after an EHR code migration. What should be validated before redesigning the clinical service?
Answer: The mapping from the new codes to the measure numerator.
Reason: The apparent decline may reflect corrupted measurement.
Source: CMS · Developing measure specifications · https://mmshub-impl.cms.gov/measure-lifecycle/measure-specification/develop-specification/overview

Topic: Using incident reports as learning signals
Prompt: What does a voluntary incident reporting system directly count?
Answer: Events that someone recognized and submitted.
Reason: Many events go unrecognized or unreported.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Measurement of patient safety · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/measurement-patient-safety

Topic: Using incident reports as learning signals
Prompt: A ward staff member reports a near miss from yesterday. What does the single report reliably establish for improvement work?
Answer: A specific hazard or event is available for investigation.
Reason: It does not indicate how often comparable events occur.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Measurement of patient safety · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/measurement-patient-safety

Topic: Using incident reports as learning signals
Prompt: After anonymous online reporting begins, near-miss submissions triple. What measurement change could explain the increase without a change in actual hazards?
Answer: Staff may now report a greater fraction of events.
Reason: The reporting channel changed ascertainment.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Measurement of patient safety · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/measurement-patient-safety

Topic: Using incident reports as learning signals
Prompt: Why is a denominator alone insufficient to estimate true harm incidence from voluntary reports?
Answer: The numerator can miss an unknown fraction of harms.
Reason: Ascertain events systematically as well as defining the population.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Measurement of patient safety · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/measurement-patient-safety

Topic: Using incident reports as learning signals
Prompt: A unit needs an estimate of medication harm per 100 admissions and suspects severe underreporting. Which additional approach could improve ascertainment?
Answer: Systematic review of a defined sample of admissions using a consistent injury definition.
Reason: This supplies an independent source of potential events and a denominator.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Measurement of patient safety · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/measurement-patient-safety

Topic: Using incident reports as learning signals
Prompt: Which two processes can change the number of incident reports?
Answer: How often events occur and how often they are recognized and reported.
Reason: Consider both before drawing conclusions.
Source: AHRQ PSNet · Measurement of patient safety · https://psnet.ahrq.gov/primer/measurement-patient-safety

Topic: Identifying implementation barriers with the people doing the work
Prompt: Why include frontline staff on an improvement team?
Answer: They know how the process actually operates and where failures occur.
Reason: Patients may identify additional burdens or barriers.
Source: IHI · Forming the improvement team · https://www.ihi.org/library/model-for-improvement/forming-team

Topic: Identifying implementation barriers with the people doing the work
Prompt: A senior leader funds a new referral workflow, but no one consulted the people receiving referrals. Whose perspective is most immediately missing?
Answer: The staff who must receive, process and act on the referrals.
Reason: Include them in mapping and testing the workflow.
Source: IHI · Forming the improvement team · https://www.ihi.org/library/model-for-improvement/forming-team

Topic: Identifying implementation barriers with the people doing the work
Prompt: Frontline staff agree on a solution but cannot authorize needed cross-department access. What different role is required?
Answer: An accountable sponsor who can resolve the organizational barrier.
Reason: Expertise in the workflow and authority to remove barriers can belong to different people.
Source: IHI · Forming the improvement team · https://www.ihi.org/library/model-for-improvement/forming-team

Topic: Identifying implementation barriers with the people doing the work
Prompt: Before assuming teams are resistant to a new workflow, what should an improvement lead find out?
Answer: What prevents staff from carrying out the task in actual practice.
Reason: Observe work and invite feedback.
Source: IHI · Forming the improvement team · https://www.ihi.org/library/model-for-improvement/forming-team

Topic: Identifying implementation barriers with the people doing the work
Prompt: Night staff support a new interpreter-assisted discharge process but do not have access to the service number. What is the most direct change?
Answer: Provide reliable after-hours access at the point of discharge.
Reason: Additional persuasion does not supply the resource.
Source: IHI · Forming the improvement team · https://www.ihi.org/library/model-for-improvement/forming-team

Topic: Identifying implementation barriers with the people doing the work
Prompt: Staff have the service number and working equipment but disagree about who initiates the call. Which change addresses this barrier?
Answer: Assign the task to a defined role and confirm it in the workflow.
Reason: The barrier is ownership.
Source: IHI · Forming the improvement team · https://www.ihi.org/library/model-for-improvement/forming-team

Topic: Identifying implementation barriers with the people doing the work
Prompt: What information should a change leader seek before spreading a pilot across a hospital?
Answer: Evidence about its effects, feasibility and unintended consequences under representative conditions.
Reason: Include the people affected by the spread.
Source: IHI · Forming the improvement team · https://www.ihi.org/library/model-for-improvement/forming-team

Topic: Identifying implementation barriers with the people doing the work
Prompt: A new version works across shifts. Weeks after the original champion leaves, completion declines. What should leadership examine?
Answer: Whether ownership, training, feedback and resources were embedded in routine work.
Reason: A successful pilot may still lack a sustainable operating process.
Source: IHI · Forming the improvement team · https://www.ihi.org/library/model-for-improvement/forming-team

Topic: Choosing care whose likely benefit justifies its burdens
Prompt: What clinical question should you ask before repeating a laboratory test?
Answer: Would the new result change a decision for this patient?
Reason: A repeat test can add cost, discomfort and downstream investigation.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Choosing care whose likely benefit justifies its burdens
Prompt: A transfer patient has a verified potassium result from ten minutes ago, is stable and has had no intervening treatment. What should you check before redrawing it by routine?
Answer: Whether the existing result already answers the clinical question.
Reason: Use available reliable information when no new result would change care.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Choosing care whose likely benefit justifies its burdens
Prompt: Another transfer patient received emergency treatment for severe hyperkalemia after the last potassium measurement. Why does a repeat potassium now have value?
Answer: It shows the response to treatment and guides the next action.
Reason: The earlier result predates a clinically important intervention.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Choosing care whose likely benefit justifies its burdens
Prompt: When deciding whether to repeat an outside imaging study, what should the receiving team first establish?
Answer: Whether an accessible study of adequate quality already answers the current question.
Reason: A new institution alone is insufficient reason for a new exposure.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Choosing care whose likely benefit justifies its burdens
Prompt: A stable patient brings a recent readable CT answering the consultant's question. What is the least burdensome next step?
Reason: Review may provide the needed information without additional radiation.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Choosing care whose likely benefit justifies its burdens
Prompt: Another patient's outside images are unreadable, and an urgent treatment choice depends on the finding. What makes obtaining adequate imaging reasonable?
Answer: The previous study cannot answer the current decision.
Reason: Consider the safest timely way to obtain the required information.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Choosing care whose likely benefit justifies its burdens
Prompt: What patient-level benefit should a clinician identify before recommending an additional diagnostic service?
Answer: A plausible way the information will improve a decision or outcome.
Reason: Cost and potential harms also matter.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Choosing care whose likely benefit justifies its burdens
Prompt: A clinician discloses ownership of a facility. An indicated test will determine which of two treatments is appropriate. How should the clinician present the referral?
Answer: Explain the clinical indication, the financial interest and reasonable alternatives.
Reason: The patient can make an informed choice about where to obtain a clinically useful service.
Source: AMA Code of Medical Ethics · Physician self-referral · https://code-medical-ethics.ama-assn.org/ethics-opinions/physician-self-referral

Topic: Investigating differences in who benefits from a service
Prompt: A clinic changes its scheduling system. Which denominators allow a fair assessment of completion across language groups?
Answer: Eligible patients in each language group during each period.
Reason: Counting only people who completed the visit hides barriers to access.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Checking whether a decision reflects a patient's own priorities
Prompt: What information is necessary to judge whether a preference-sensitive decision fits the patient?
Answer: The patient's informed priorities for the relevant outcomes.
Reason: The same trade-off may be acceptable to one person and unacceptable to another.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Checking whether a decision reflects a patient's own priorities
Prompt: Two options offer similar survival. A patient prioritizes staying alert enough to care for a child. Which outcome deserves particular attention in comparing options?
Answer: The expected effect on alertness and daily function.
Reason: The patient's goal identifies which trade-off needs discussion.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Checking whether a decision reflects a patient's own priorities
Prompt: Another patient facing the same options prioritizes relief of otherwise intolerable symptoms and accepts drowsiness. Which outcome should guide this comparison?
Answer: Expected symptom relief, with the accepted sedation trade-off.
Reason: The patient's priorities changed even though the treatment options did not.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Checking whether a decision reflects a patient's own priorities
Prompt: A patient asks you to recommend one of two reasonable treatments. What should you elicit before making a tailored recommendation?
Answer: Which outcomes and burdens matter most to them.
Reason: A clinician can recommend a plan after understanding the patient's priorities.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Checking whether a decision reflects a patient's own priorities
Prompt: A patient wants to keep working during cancer treatment. What practical question helps compare two similarly effective regimens?
Answer: How would each regimen's visits and adverse effects affect the patient's work?
Reason: Clarify the impact the patient wants to minimize.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Checking whether a decision reflects a patient's own priorities
Prompt: A patient says both preserving hand function and having the shortest recovery matter. The options favor different goals. What should the clinician clarify next?
Answer: Which trade-off the patient would accept if both goals cannot be achieved together.
Reason: A preference list alone leaves the decision unresolved.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Checking whether a decision reflects a patient's own priorities
Prompt: Which comparison directly assesses whether delivered care matches a patient's goals?
Answer: Compare the actual care with the patient's informed goals at the time of the decision.
Reason: A completed preferences form alone does not establish concordance.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Checking whether a decision reflects a patient's own priorities
Prompt: A patient consistently requested home support, but a planning meeting presumed nursing-home placement without discussing alternatives. What should be reviewed?
Answer: Whether the team explored a feasible plan consistent with the patient's stated goal.
Reason: Review the assumptions and available support with the patient.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Checking whether a decision reflects a patient's own priorities
Prompt: After learning what home care would require, the same capable patient expressly chooses residential care. How should the team interpret the change?
Answer: Assess the plan against the patient's updated informed preference.
Reason: Record why the goal changed and share it with the care team.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Locating delays in a patient's path through care
Prompt: How do you locate a bottleneck when a total wait contains several steps?
Answer: Measure the elapsed time in each step.
Reason: A total duration alone cannot identify where the time was spent.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Locating delays in a patient's path through care
Prompt: In the urgent-clinic record, which interval accounts for most of the time before the result?
Reason: The second interval takes 20 minutes.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Locating delays in a patient's path through care
Prompt: In this second clinic, which interval accounts for most of the same total wait?
Reason: The first interval takes 15 minutes.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Locating delays in a patient's path through care
Prompt: For a project to reduce the time until a patient receives an indicated medicine, what event should end the measured interval?
Reason: Time of ordering measures an earlier part of the process.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Locating delays in a patient's path through care
Prompt: On an audit, orders are usually signed promptly but doses arrive late. Which interval should the team examine next?
Reason: Timing the later stages can locate an actionable delay.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Locating delays in a patient's path through care
Prompt: After bedside delivery is introduced, doses follow signed orders promptly, but patients still wait before anyone recognizes the need. Which interval now deserves review?
Answer: First qualifying finding to clinical recognition or order.
Reason: The remaining delay happens upstream of delivery.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Locating delays in a patient's path through care
Prompt: Which percentile helps assess delays among the longest-waiting patients when the median looks acceptable?
Answer: An upper percentile, such as the 90th percentile.
Reason: Report it alongside the median and denominator.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Locating delays in a patient's path through care
Prompt: After a pilot, the median wait falls from 40 to 30 minutes but the 90th percentile rises from 95 to 130 minutes. Which patients warrant closer review?
Reason: The typical wait improved while the upper end worsened.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Locating delays in a patient's path through care
Prompt: After a second pilot, both median and 90th-percentile waits fall, but patients who left before being seen were excluded. Which group must be counted to assess timely access?
Answer: Patients who left before receiving care.
Reason: The recorded waits describe only those who stayed.
Source: AHRQ · Six domains of healthcare quality · https://www.ahrq.gov/talkingquality/measures/six-domains.html

Topic: Interpreting a localization study for a missing surgical item
Prompt: What feature of a surgical sponge is designed to make it visible on an x-ray?
Reason: Ordinary cloth by itself can be difficult to distinguish from soft tissue.

Topic: Interpreting a localization study for a missing surgical item
Prompt: A postoperative film shows an unexpected folded radiopaque strip in the operative area. Which feature makes a retained sponge a consideration?
Answer: The strip may represent a sponge marker.

Topic: Interpreting a localization study for a missing surgical item
Prompt: An unmarked nonradiopaque dressing is missing and a plain film appears clear. Can the clear film exclude retention of that dressing?
Answer: No. The item may be radiographically invisible.
Reason: The imaging method must be capable of detecting the missing material.

Topic: Interpreting a localization study for a missing surgical item
Prompt: Before relying on a negative localization image for a missing radiopaque item, what should the team check about the field of view?
Answer: That it includes the entire area where the item could remain.
Reason: Even a conspicuous marker can lie outside the image.
Source: American College of Surgeons · Prevention of unintentionally retained surgical items · https://www.facs.org/about-acs/statements/prevention-of-unintentionally-retained-surgical-items-after-surgery/

Topic: Interpreting a localization study for a missing surgical item
Prompt: A sponge is missing after a pelvic procedure. A negative film ends above the operative pelvis. What does the image establish about the pelvis?
Answer: It does not evaluate the operative pelvis.
Reason: Tell the team about the incomplete coverage and obtain the indicated evaluation.
Source: American College of Surgeons · Prevention of unintentionally retained surgical items · https://www.facs.org/about-acs/statements/prevention-of-unintentionally-retained-surgical-items-after-surgery/

Topic: Interpreting a localization study for a missing surgical item
Prompt: Another patient has a film covering the whole operative field. The radiologist identifies an unexplained sponge marker in it. What should the clinician do with this finding?
Answer: Notify the operating team promptly to localize and address the suspected retained item.
Reason: A positive finding warrants action regardless of the earlier count.
Source: American College of Surgeons · Prevention of unintentionally retained surgical items · https://www.facs.org/about-acs/statements/prevention-of-unintentionally-retained-surgical-items-after-surgery/

Topic: Interpreting a localization study for a missing surgical item
Prompt: When might an operating team need to defer a standard surgical-item check?
Answer: When completing it immediately would obstruct lifesaving care.
Reason: The team must keep track of the unresolved check.
Source: American College of Surgeons · Prevention of unintentionally retained surgical items · https://www.facs.org/about-acs/statements/prevention-of-unintentionally-retained-surgical-items-after-surgery/

Topic: Interpreting a localization study for a missing surgical item
Prompt: A patient is exsanguinating, and immediate hemorrhage control cannot safely wait for a count discrepancy to be investigated. What takes priority at that moment?
Reason: Communicate the outstanding discrepancy during resuscitation.
Source: American College of Surgeons · Prevention of unintentionally retained surgical items · https://www.facs.org/about-acs/statements/prevention-of-unintentionally-retained-surgical-items-after-surgery/

Topic: Interpreting a localization study for a missing surgical item
Prompt: Hemorrhage is controlled. A count skipped during the emergency remains unresolved. What should the team do now?

Topic: CARS · Humanities · The solitary line
Prompt:
The first thing an editor proposed to cut from my little volume of sea poems was the line that consisted entirely of the word “again.” She penciled the word onto the end of the previous line and read the passage aloud. I had to admit that her reading was indistinguishable from mine. We paused in the same place and stressed the same syllables. She considered the experiment conclusive. So did I, though I thought we had established something quite different.

On the page, the previous line ended with a father telling his daughter that the tide had taken her boat. The reader might have supposed that the loss was the occasion for the poem. On reaching the short line, one had to revise that supposition. Apparently there had been other boats, or other losses that the father put in the same class. Of course the editor's version disclosed that history too. What it took away was a small interval in which the reader could be honestly mistaken. A pause in a reading can sometimes do this work. But in our two readings neither of us made such a pause. Knowing what was coming, we carried the earlier words forward to meet it.

There is an old classroom exercise in which a poem is printed as prose and students must guess where the poet put the breaks. I used to give high marks for accurate guesses. Then a student divided a description of a kitchen just before the word “knife.” In the original the knife lay harmlessly among the forks. In her version the preceding line left an elderly woman alone at the kitchen table, and the knife arrived as a small threat. She had guessed incorrectly, but she could tell me precisely what her arrangement made a reader expect. The student who had reproduced the original arrangement could tell me only that it looked right.

It would be foolish to conclude that a poem improves with the number of reasonable mistakes it invites. There are poems in which every line arrives at its close as neatly as a boat comes into its berth. The pleasure of those endings lies partly in having foreseen them. Nor does a short line work its spell upon a reader who already sees the whole page at a glance. My volume will find such readers, and I shall have to let them pass through that interval at their own speed.

I kept the line, and accepted the editor's next suggestion, which was to remove a full stop after it. Without the stop, the solitary word could glance backward at the loss while already belonging to the description of the returning tide below. It would be odd to say that I thereby preserved the poem exactly as I first imagined it. My editor helped me find another use for the space whose first use she had almost erased.

Choices:
It instructs every reader to observe a longer audible pause.
It allows a first interpretation to form before the next line alters it.
It removes uncertainty about how many boats the daughter owned.
It isolates the father's speech from the rest of the poem.
Answer: It allows a first interpretation to form before the next line alters it.
Reason: The reader can briefly take the loss as a single occasion before discovering a history of loss.

Topic: CARS · Social science · Lending a ladder
Prompt:
When a resident of the square needed a ladder, she used to knock on the door of a man who painted houses. He kept three ladders and usually had one to spare. A researcher visiting the square called this a system of exchange. She assumed that the painter remembered his loans and could one day call in an equivalent number of favors. When he died, however, nobody could recall his having asked for much of anything. The researcher might have concluded that this was a remarkably poor system for keeping accounts. The painter's daughter suggested that she had been looking at the wrong account altogether.

Her father liked being the person who could supply a ladder. Children knew his name before they were tall enough to carry one. New residents learned which bell to ring. A neighbor who had borrowed the longest ladder said he had returned it with a bag of plums. The painter took two plums and sent the rest upstairs to a family who had recently moved in. Perhaps he expected the family to repay him. But the daughter recalled that the painter did not even introduce himself when he brought up the bag. The neighbor who supplied it, on the other hand, still told the story twenty years later.

One could call that durable recollection a kind of payment. Yet the word would conceal a distinction that matters. In a debt, the person owed can ordinarily say what would count as settling it. A painter owed a day's labor may forgive the day, or ask for two afternoons instead. The painter of the square could do neither with a story. He could encourage his neighbor to tell it, but he could not decide when that neighbor had remembered him sufficiently. The good he obtained from lending depended on someone else's continuing freedom over what to make of it.

The square now owns a communal ladder kept in a shed. There is a sign-out sheet, and the resident who returns the ladder late loses borrowing privileges for a week. Some older residents regard the shed as a chilly successor to the painter's kitchen. They forget that some newcomers had been too shy to ring his bell. The sign-out sheet tells a newcomer exactly what she owes and when she will be free of the obligation. A precise rule can be a considerable kindness to someone who does not yet know how a neighborhood interprets a favor.

If we count ladders carried home, the shed might easily prove the better institution. If we count stories, the painter might win. Neither result could tell us what would happen if the shed employed an attendant whose job was to strike up conversations. Someone paid to welcome you can become a friend. But the terms of employment can purchase only the greeting. Whether the meeting gives either person a standing in the other's life is a question that remains open after both have done everything required of them.

What distinction does the narrator draw between a debt and the social benefit the painter gained?
Choices:
A debt must be paid in goods, while a social benefit takes the form of labor.
A debt always creates resentment, whereas a favor always creates friendship.
A creditor can specify what settles a debt, while the painter cannot prescribe the meaning of a neighbor's recollection.
A debt exists between strangers, while a neighbor can incur only a social obligation.
Answer: A creditor can specify what settles a debt, while the painter cannot prescribe the meaning of a neighbor's recollection.
Reason: The comparison turns on control over the conditions of settlement.

Topic: CARS · Social science · Lending a ladder
Prompt:
When a resident of the square needed a ladder, she used to knock on the door of a man who painted houses. He kept three ladders and usually had one to spare. A researcher visiting the square called this a system of exchange. She assumed that the painter remembered his loans and could one day call in an equivalent number of favors. When he died, however, nobody could recall his having asked for much of anything. The researcher might have concluded that this was a remarkably poor system for keeping accounts. The painter's daughter suggested that she had been looking at the wrong account altogether.

Her father liked being the person who could supply a ladder. Children knew his name before they were tall enough to carry one. New residents learned which bell to ring. A neighbor who had borrowed the longest ladder said he had returned it with a bag of plums. The painter took two plums and sent the rest upstairs to a family who had recently moved in. Perhaps he expected the family to repay him. But the daughter recalled that the painter did not even introduce himself when he brought up the bag. The neighbor who supplied it, on the other hand, still told the story twenty years later.

One could call that durable recollection a kind of payment. Yet the word would conceal a distinction that matters. In a debt, the person owed can ordinarily say what would count as settling it. A painter owed a day's labor may forgive the day, or ask for two afternoons instead. The painter of the square could do neither with a story. He could encourage his neighbor to tell it, but he could not decide when that neighbor had remembered him sufficiently. The good he obtained from lending depended on someone else's continuing freedom over what to make of it.

The square now owns a communal ladder kept in a shed. There is a sign-out sheet, and the resident who returns the ladder late loses borrowing privileges for a week. Some older residents regard the shed as a chilly successor to the painter's kitchen. They forget that some newcomers had been too shy to ring his bell. The sign-out sheet tells a newcomer exactly what she owes and when she will be free of the obligation. A precise rule can be a considerable kindness to someone who does not yet know how a neighborhood interprets a favor.

If we count ladders carried home, the shed might easily prove the better institution. If we count stories, the painter might win. Neither result could tell us what would happen if the shed employed an attendant whose job was to strike up conversations. Someone paid to welcome you can become a friend. But the terms of employment can purchase only the greeting. Whether the meeting gives either person a standing in the other's life is a question that remains open after both have done everything required of them.

The painter did not tell the family who he was.

Topic: CARS · Humanities · The missing room
Prompt:
Halfway through an old detective story, a woman leaves a dining room by a door that the author has forgotten to provide. I owe this discovery to a carpenter who came to our reading group once and never returned. He had drawn the house on the back of a grocery receipt. The exterior walls closed neatly, the stairs took up a credible amount of space, and the woman was apparently standing in a cupboard. The rest of us had spent the evening discussing her reasons for leaving dinner. We felt vaguely injured by the receipt.

It was suggested that an author might fairly be charged rent only for the rooms the story actually uses. Nobody had inquired where the family kept its coal. Why should anyone ask what lay beyond that particular door? The carpenter had an unexpectedly literary answer. The woman later says that she heard the last part of the dinner conversation from the passage. Whether the dining room opened onto that passage bore on the truth of what she said. Our interpretations of her conduct had quietly assumed a house in which it was possible to listen.

Over the next month our group acquired a taste for drawing plans. It was a disagreeable month. In a short story about a visit to a dying brother, we spent a quarter of an hour fitting a bathroom between a bedroom and an attic staircase. One member proposed shifting the staircase. Another abolished the bathroom. Either alteration left the visit exactly as painful as it had been before. We had learned how to find an inconsistency without learning when it cost the story anything.

I would give the carpenter's receipt a place in an edition of the detective story, though I would put it at the end. A reader should first have a chance to trust the woman. Seeing the plan in advance turns an ordinary remark about overhearing into an examination question about architecture. Read afterward, the plan gives a reader an interesting choice. One can amend the house, as an editor might amend a misspelling, and continue to believe her. Or one can let the walls stand and wonder who supplied the woman with the words she claimed to have overheard. I doubt that the author intended this choice. I find it a real one all the same.

Our carpenter sent us a note in response to the minutes of that meeting. He regretted that we had all taken the trouble to draw houses. He himself had started with the woman's assertion about hearing. A dining room door had been the cheapest part of the assertion to check. If she had claimed to recognize a distant voice, he wrote, he would have wanted the opinion of a singer. I have kept his receipt in my copy of the book. When I lend the book, I leave the receipt in its envelope, and leave the envelope unsealed.

Why does the carpenter consider this particular doorway worth investigating?
Choices:
It would reveal how many servants the house could employ.
Its location bears on whether the woman could have heard what she reports.
The novel offers unusually exact exterior measurements.
The doorway appears in the title of the book.
Answer: Its location bears on whether the woman could have heard what she reports.
Reason: The woman's later assertion depends on an acoustic path from the dining room to the passage.
Source: Original passage and item · AAMC CARS framework · https://students-residents.aamc.org/whats-mcat-exam/critical-analysis-and-reasoning-skills-section-overview

Bus fares had to be paid out of the foreman's hiring budget.
Some applicants could not reach the queue soon enough to receive an early interview.
Every applicant arriving after six lost the right to an interview.

Topic: CARS · Humanities · The repeated word
Prompt:
An editor preparing a new edition of a novel found the word “harbour” written twice on the last page of the author's manuscript. In the first printed edition the second occurrence was gone. The editor put it back. To a reader who asked why, she replied that it was her business to let the author speak. Yet the deletion might have been the author's own correction in proof. No proof sheets survive. The editor had made a choice on good evidence, but her account of that choice sounded more certain than her evidence allowed.

The reader's proposed remedy was an edition that reproduced the manuscript photographically. Nobody could then accuse an editor of silently changing a word. At the library they laid a photograph beside the manuscript. A crease in the paper made one of the letters look considerably darker in the photograph. On the original, the reader could tilt the sheet and see that the dark stroke was a shadow. He conceded that a photograph answered some questions about the manuscript very well. It had also raised a new question that could be settled only by returning to the sheet. Even deciding which instrument would give unmediated access to the novel seemed to require the judgment of an editor.

Years earlier, a theater company had asked visitors to read the last page aloud. Almost everyone paused at the repeated word. In the recordings the pause sounded like a person returning to a place she had left. This pleased the editor, who considered return the novel's great subject. It did not please her enough to count as proof. The actors had worked from copies in which she herself had restored the repetition. Their response showed what the repetition could do to a listener. It could tell her very little about who had deleted it.

She finally printed the repeated word in the text and added a note giving the reading of the first edition. The note was a single line. A colleague objected that a single line could hardly convey the hours of comparison the decision had required. That objection mistook the work the note had to do. A purchaser need not learn every step by which an editor had reached a decision in order to try reading the page the other way. For this particular difference, a short note put the experiment within reach of anyone with the book.

There are disagreements for which that economy would fail. If two surviving chapters arranged a sequence of events differently, a list of altered page numbers might leave the alternative nearly impossible to experience. Printing both chapters could be justified. The appropriate space for an alternative depends less on the number of scholarly hours expended than on what the reader must do to recover it. A useful edition can express a preference while making the cost of disagreeing with it reasonably small.

Why did the reader initially propose a photographic edition?
Choices:
To preserve evidence of the author's later corrections in proof.
To remove the possibility of undetected verbal intervention by an editor.
To reproduce the actors' pauses more accurately.
To establish the first printed edition as the authoritative text.
Answer: To remove the possibility of undetected verbal intervention by an editor.
Reason: The reader wanted to prevent silent changes. Nothing suggests that the missing proofs could be recovered.

The editor put it back. To a reader who asked why, she replied that it was her business to let the author speak. Yet the deletion might have been the author's own correction in proof. No proof sheets survive. The editor had made a choice on good evidence, but her account of that choice sounded more certain than her evidence allowed.

The reader's proposed remedy was an edition that reproduced the manuscript photographically. Nobody could then accuse an editor of silently changing a word. At the library they laid a photograph beside the manuscript. A crease in the paper made one of the letters look considerably darker in the photograph. On the original, the reader could tilt the sheet and see that the dark stroke was a shadow. He conceded that a photograph answered some questions about the manuscript very well. It had also raised a new question that could be settled only by returning to the sheet. Even deciding which instrument would give unmediated access to the novel seemed to require the judgment of an editor.

Years earlier, a theater company had asked visitors to read the last page aloud. Almost everyone paused at the repeated word. In the recordings the pause sounded like a person returning to a place she had left. This pleased the editor, who considered return the novel's great subject. It did not please her enough to count as proof. The actors had worked from copies in which she herself had restored the repetition. Their response showed what the repetition could do to a listener. It could tell her very little about who had deleted it.

She finally printed the repeated word in the text and added a note giving the reading of the first edition. The note was a single line. A colleague objected that a single line could hardly convey the hours of comparison the decision had required. That objection mistook the work the note had to do. A purchaser need not learn every step by which an editor had reached a decision in order to try reading the page the other way. For this particular difference, a short note put the experiment within reach of anyone with the book.

There are disagreements for which that economy would fail. If two surviving chapters arranged a sequence of events differently, a list of altered page numbers might leave the alternative nearly impossible to experience. Printing both chapters could be justified. The appropriate space for an alternative depends less on the number of scholarly hours expended than on what the reader must do to recover it. A useful edition can express a preference while making the cost of disagreeing with it reasonably small.

A signed proof turns up with an instruction in the author's hand to delete the second occurrence. Which inference changes most directly?
Choices:
The repetition could create a sense of return when read aloud.
A crease may affect the appearance of a photographed letter.
The source of the deletion can now be attributed with greater confidence.
A one-word alternative can be tested with a short note.
Answer: The source of the deletion can now be attributed with greater confidence.
Reason: The proof bears on authorship of the deletion. The effects of the two readings can still be compared.

Topic: CARS · Social science · Buying at dawn
Prompt:
A fishing town tried selling the day's catch without attaching the boat's name to the boxes. The auctioneer called it an experiment in judging fish by fish. For years, a few boats had fetched high prices even on mornings when their catches looked much like their neighbors'. Buyers said that the difference was deserved. The crews of those boats packed their fish in ice sooner. By noon a difference invisible at the quay would become obvious in a shop. Crews without a famous name had a different complaint. Cooling their own fish just as quickly did them little good if no buyer would look in their direction.

During the trial the auctioneer gave each box a number. A buyer could open a box, examine its contents and pay whatever seemed fitting. The harbor office kept the list of numbers and boats so that a shop could still report a spoiled purchase. On the first morning, the range of prices narrowed. Some crews hailed the change as proof that their better-known neighbors had been selling an expensive name. Their neighbors pointed to the very same figures as proof that careful work went unrewarded once its author was hidden.

A reporter proposed to settle the matter by visiting the shops that afternoon. If fish from the famous boats kept better, surely that would vindicate the old prices. The visits would certainly be worth making. But suppose she did find such a difference. She would have learned something about the information a name had carried before the trial. She would still know little about what an unfamiliar crew could accomplish under arrangements that allowed it to profit from equally careful work. For that question, the morning of the change was a particularly bad day to choose. Every box then on sale had been packed under habits formed during the old auction.

The harbor office eventually offered an additional service. Buyers could request a record of afternoon inspections for the last ten boxes packed by any crew, identified by a persistent code. After several months, a crew with a poor early record began fetching higher prices following a run of favorable inspections. The auctioneer celebrated the return of judgment by particulars. Yet no buyer who consulted the record was judging one box by its contents alone. Ten previous boxes had entered the bargain too.

It would be a mistake to treat that dependence as an embarrassment. A shop buying at dawn needs evidence about a condition it will face at noon. The choice at the quay is partly a choice about which histories deserve to travel with a box. A familiar name carries a history whose beginning may be beyond anyone's memory and whose errors may be costly to challenge. A short inspection record can be revised by later catches, although it too may mislead when an inspector visits one shop much later in the day than another. Asking how a history can be corrected gives the town a more useful question than asking how to dispense with history altogether.

Why did the harbor office keep the list matching numbers to boats during the first trial?
Choices:
To show bidders the last ten inspections before they set a price.
To let buyers report a spoiled box to an office that could trace its source.
To ensure each crew received its previous price on the first day.
To tell reporters which crew had received the most favorable bids.
Answer: To let buyers report a spoiled box to an office that could trace its source.
Reason: The matching list preserved traceability after purchase. The ten-box record was a later change.

Reason: It is preferred in most clinical situations when hands are not visibly soiled.

Topic: Selecting and measuring hand hygiene practices

Prompt: Two shifts recorded 9 actions at 10 opportunities and 30 actions at 50 opportunities. What was combined observed adherence?

Topic: Finding the null value on an effect scale
Prompt: What calculation defines the null value of an effect measure comparing two groups?
Answer: Evaluate the measure when the two population outcomes are equal.
Reason: Dividing equal nonzero risks gives one. Subtracting equal risks gives zero.
Source: ICH · E9 Statistical Principles for Clinical Trials · https://database.ich.org/sites/default/files/E9_Guideline.pdf

Topic: Finding the null value on an effect scale
Prompt: A trial plots intervention risk minus control risk, in percentage points. At which value would an interval contain equal population risks?
Reason: The axis reports a difference. Two equal risks subtract to zero.
Source: ICH · E9 Statistical Principles for Clinical Trials · https://database.ich.org/sites/default/files/E9_Guideline.pdf

Topic: Reading confidence limits on different effect scales
Prompt: For a two-sided 95% interval, what feature lets you reject the corresponding point null at 5% using the matching test?
Answer: The interval excludes the null value.
Reason: The interval and test must use compatible assumptions and methods.
Source: ICH · E9 Statistical Principles for Clinical Trials · https://database.ich.org/sites/default/files/E9_Guideline.pdf

Topic: Reading confidence limits on different effect scales
Prompt: A trial reports a mortality risk ratio of 0.74 with a 95% interval from 0.59 to 0.94. Does it exclude equal risks?
Answer: Yes. The upper limit is below one.
Reason: Every value in the interval corresponds to a lower risk in the numerator group.
Source: ICH · E9 Statistical Principles for Clinical Trials · https://database.ich.org/sites/default/files/E9_Guideline.pdf

Topic: Reading confidence limits on different effect scales
Prompt: The 95% interval for an absolute reduction in admissions ranges from −1 to +6 percentage points. Is a reduction established at the matching two-sided 5% level?
Answer: No. The interval includes zero and also allows a small increase.
Reason: A favorable point estimate alone cannot settle the direction.
Source: ICH · E9 Statistical Principles for Clinical Trials · https://database.ich.org/sites/default/files/E9_Guideline.pdf

Topic: Using uncertainty to interpret a trial comparison
Prompt: What must be specified about acceptable differences before an equivalence comparison is interpreted?
Answer: The lower and upper equivalence margins.
Reason: The corresponding interval must fit within both limits to rule out differences considered too large.
Source: ICH · E9 Statistical Principles for Clinical Trials · https://database.ich.org/sites/default/files/E9_Guideline.pdf

Topic: Using uncertainty to interpret a trial comparison
Prompt: A committee treats a nonsignificant 8-week risk difference as proof of interchangeability. Its 90% interval is −9 to +7 points and its equivalence margins are ±3. Does this support interchangeability?
Answer: No. The interval extends beyond both margins.
Reason: Failing to reject a zero difference can coexist with substantial uncertainty.
Source: ICH · E9 Statistical Principles for Clinical Trials · https://database.ich.org/sites/default/files/E9_Guideline.pdf

Topic: Counting opportunities for false positives
Prompt: One prespecified endpoint is tested at alpha 0.05. Under its true null, what is the nominal probability of a false positive in this analysis?
Reason: Only one test belongs to the comparison being described.
Source: FDA · Multiple Endpoints in Clinical Trials · https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/multiple-endpoints-clinical-trials

Topic: Counting opportunities for false positives
Prompt: Two independent endpoints are each tested at 0.05, and both null hypotheses are true. What is the chance of at least one false positive?
Reason: The chance of neither is 0.95 squared. Subtract that result from one.
Source: FDA · Multiple Endpoints in Clinical Trials · https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/multiple-endpoints-clinical-trials

Topic: Controlling false positives across several endpoints
Prompt: How does a Bonferroni rule set the per-test cutoff for a family of m comparisons?
Answer: Divide the desired family-wise alpha by m.
Reason: This bounds the probability of any false rejection without requiring independence.
Source: FDA · Multiple Endpoints in Clinical Trials · https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/multiple-endpoints-clinical-trials

Topic: Controlling false positives across several endpoints
Prompt: Four primary comparisons share family-wise alpha 0.05 equally under Bonferroni. One raw p-value is 0.009. Does it pass?
Reason: The raw p-value is below the adjusted cutoff.
Source: FDA · Multiple Endpoints in Clinical Trials · https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/multiple-endpoints-clinical-trials

Topic: Controlling false positives across several endpoints
Prompt: A paper declared five primary comparisons and prespecified Bonferroni control at 0.05. Its smallest raw p-value is 0.018. How many comparisons pass?
Reason: The cutoff is 0.01. The smallest raw p-value is already larger.
Source: FDA · Multiple Endpoints in Clinical Trials · https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/multiple-endpoints-clinical-trials

Topic: Reading a trial's fixed testing order
Prompt: In a prespecified fixed-sequence procedure that tests each endpoint at 0.05, when can the next endpoint be tested confirmatorily?
Answer: After all preceding hypotheses in the sequence have been rejected.
Reason: The fixed order controls which results may support confirmatory claims.
Source: FDA · Multiple Endpoints in Clinical Trials · https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/multiple-endpoints-clinical-trials

Topic: Reading a trial's fixed testing order
Prompt: A trial tests mortality first, then admission, stopping at the first failed test. Mortality gives p=0.14 and admission p=0.002. What status does the admission finding have?
Answer: Descriptive or exploratory under this plan.
Reason: The first test did not open the gate for confirmatory testing of admissions.
Source: FDA · Multiple Endpoints in Clinical Trials · https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/multiple-endpoints-clinical-trials

Topic: Reading a trial's fixed testing order
Prompt: Another trial prespecified symptoms first and function second at alpha 0.05. Its p-values are 0.008 and 0.031 respectively. Does the function result meet the fixed-sequence criterion?
Answer: Yes. Both tests pass in order.
Reason: Provided the plan and tests are valid, no additional division by two is required under this procedure.

Topic: Changing precision and power in a sampling model
Prompt: For independent observations with the same population SD, how does the standard error of the mean vary with sample size n?
Answer: It is proportional to one over the square root of n.
Reason: A narrower sampling distribution generally gives more power for a fixed nonzero effect and alpha.
Source: ICH · E9 Statistical Principles for Clinical Trials · https://database.ich.org/sites/default/files/E9_Guideline.pdf

Topic: Changing precision and power in a sampling model
Prompt: A study increases independent participants from 100 to 400 with unchanged variance and effect. How does that change its standard error?
Reason: The greater precision generally raises power at the specified alternative.
Source: ICH · E9 Statistical Principles for Clinical Trials · https://database.ich.org/sites/default/files/E9_Guideline.pdf

Topic: Changing precision and power in a sampling model
Prompt: A clinic duplicates each of 100 electronic records four times and treats all 400 rows as independent. Has it gained the precision or power of enrolling 400 patients?
Answer: No. It still has 100 independent patients.
Reason: Treating exact copies as independent produces artificially small standard errors.
Source: ICH · E9 Statistical Principles for Clinical Trials · https://database.ich.org/sites/default/files/E9_Guideline.pdf

Topic: Planning a trial for a specified difference
Prompt: What is statistical power for a specified alternative and analysis plan?
Answer: The probability of rejecting the null if that alternative is true.
Reason: The risk of a false negative at that alternative is one minus power.
Source: ICH · E9 Statistical Principles for Clinical Trials · https://database.ich.org/sites/default/files/E9_Guideline.pdf

Topic: Planning a trial for a specified difference
Prompt: A trial switches to a more reproducible continuous measurement that halves its outcome SD. With equal allocation, the same meaningful mean difference, alpha and power, about how many participants does it now need?
Answer: About one quarter as many, under the usual two-group mean approximation.
Reason: Required sample size is proportional to variance. Halving SD quarters variance.
Source: ICH · E9 Statistical Principles for Clinical Trials · https://database.ich.org/sites/default/files/E9_Guideline.pdf

Topic: Judging power when recruitment or the event rate changes
Prompt: In an event-driven time-to-event trial, which count chiefly determines the information for the planned treatment comparison?
Answer: The number of observed endpoint events.
Reason: Allocation, assumptions and event timing also matter. Head count alone can be misleading.

Topic: Judging power when recruitment or the event rate changes
Prompt: A prevention trial enrolled the intended number of people but stopped at the planned calendar date with only half the required events. How does this affect interpretation of a nonsignificant result?
Answer: The study has less information and less power than planned for the target effect.
Reason: Inspect the treatment interval for benefits and harms still compatible with the data.
Source: ICH · E9 Statistical Principles for Clinical Trials · https://database.ich.org/sites/default/files/E9_Guideline.pdf

Topic: Judging power when recruitment or the event rate changes
Prompt: An otherwise similar trial experiences the same low event rate but follows the original event-driven protocol until its target number of events accrues. Does the low incidence alone imply it missed its information target?
Answer: No. The target event count was reached.
Reason: Follow-up took longer. Assess the actual interval, assumptions and completeness of observation.
Source: ICH · E9 Statistical Principles for Clinical Trials · https://database.ich.org/sites/default/files/E9_Guideline.pdf

Topic: Comparing precision of estimates
Prompt: For estimates of the same quantity, on the same scale and confidence level, what does a narrower confidence interval indicate?
Reason: It does not exclude systematic bias.
Source: ICH · E9 Statistical Principles for Clinical Trials · https://database.ich.org/sites/default/files/E9_Guideline.pdf

Topic: Comparing precision of estimates
Prompt: Two independent clinic samples have the same symptom-score SD. One CI for the mean is 8 to 12 and the other is 9.5 to 10.5. Which mean was estimated more precisely?
Reason: Its interval is one unit wide versus four.
Source: ICH · E9 Statistical Principles for Clinical Trials · https://database.ich.org/sites/default/files/E9_Guideline.pdf

Topic: Comparing precision of estimates
Prompt: A large trial reports a mean change of 5 points with 95% CI 4.9 to 5.1. A clinician tells a patient that nearly everyone improved by about 5 points. What additional information is needed?
Reason: The narrow confidence limits summarize uncertainty in the estimated mean.

Topic: Calculating expected cell counts under independence

Topic: Calculating expected cell counts under independence
Prompt: A ward screens 80 of the study's 200 participants. Across the study 50 results are positive. Under independence, how many positives are expected in that ward?

Topic: Reading power at a clinically relevant effect size
Prompt: Using the curves, which study is less likely to miss a true standardized effect of 0.4?

Topic: Reading power at a clinically relevant effect size
Prompt: Two trial designs use different sample sizes. The plot shows the test statistic under the null model for each design after standardization. At the marked cutoffs, does one design reject a true null more often?
